title: MUH Noon Conference — question bank
description: Board-style questions built from the 2026–27 MUH internal medicine noon conference lectures. Each question tests a point taught in one lecture and was checked against current guidelines; lecture points that disagreed with current evidence were left out. The first reference names the lecture and the slide(s)/transcript excerpt(s) it came from (excerpt ids match the NoonSpeak parcel files); the first link opens the lecture recording (UPMC sign-in required). Ids start with noon-NN- (NN = lecture number).

questions.topic: Albumin-corrected anion gap and the delta-delta
questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department after 5 days of epigastric pain, poor oral intake, and repeated vomiting. Temperature is 37.1°C, blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg, pulse is 108/min, and respiratory rate is 18/min. He has dry mucous membranes and temporal wasting. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium136 mEq/L
Potassium3.1 mEq/L
Chloride99 mEq/L
Bicarbonate21 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen28 mg/dL
Creatinine1.2 mg/dL
Glucose76 mg/dL
Albumin1.6 g/dL
Lactate1.4 mmol/L
β-Hydroxybutyrate5.2 mmol/L
Arterial pH7.34
Arterial PCO240 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid–base status?

options.A: Pure anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
options.B: Non–anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
options.C: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and non–anion gap metabolic acidosis
options.D: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis
options.E: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis

questions.explanation: Calculate the anion gap regardless of the bicarbonate: 136 − (99 + 21) = 16. Then correct it for albumin: 16 + 2.5 × (4.0 − 1.6) = 22, a definite gap acidosis. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO2 of 1.5 × 21 + 8 ± 2 = 37.5–41.5 mm Hg, so 40 is appropriate. For the delta-delta, add the delta gap to the measured bicarbonate: 21 + (22 − 12) = 31. Bicarbonate was high before the gap acidosis developed, revealing a coexisting metabolic alkalosis.

why_not.A: The uncorrected gap of 16 hides a true gap of 22, and a bicarbonate of 21 is far higher than a pure gap acidosis would leave (about 14).
why_not.B: The gap is elevated, clearly so after albumin correction, so this is not a non–anion gap process.
why_not.C: A coexisting non-gap acidosis would push bicarbonate below the value predicted from the gap; here it is above it.
why_not.D: Winter's formula predicts a PaCO2 of 37.5–41.5 mm Hg, so a PaCO2 of 40 is appropriate compensation.

questions.pearl: Calculate the gap regardless of bicarbonate, correct it for albumin, then add the delta gap to HCO3 to unmask a hidden metabolic alkalosis.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 1: ABG Interpretation — Dr. Rachel Givelber, 7/23/2026 (slides 8, 11, 26; transcript excerpt 01_P012)

questions.topic: Respiratory alkalosis with anion gap metabolic acidosis
questions.stem:
A 34-year-old woman with depression and chronic migraine is brought to the emergency department by her roommate, who found her confused at home. Temperature is 38.2°C, blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, pulse is 116/min, respiratory rate is 32/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The lungs are clear. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium140 mEq/L
Potassium3.6 mEq/L
Chloride104 mEq/L
Bicarbonate12 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen14 mg/dL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Glucose98 mg/dL
Albumin4.0 g/dL
Lactate1.3 mmol/L
Arterial pH7.50
Arterial PCO216 mm Hg
Arterial PO2118 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following tests is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: pH 7.50 with a PaCO2 of 16 means pH and PCO2 moved in opposite directions: a primary respiratory alkalosis. If acute, bicarbonate should fall about 2 per 10 mm Hg drop in PCO2 (to about 19), so a bicarbonate of 12 means a coexisting metabolic acidosis, and the anion gap is 24. Septic patients often have both disorders, but the metabolic acidosis usually dominates, and her lactate is normal. A profound respiratory alkalosis plus an anion gap metabolic acidosis should make you think of salicylate poisoning; salicylates powerfully stimulate breathing, so check a salicylate level.

why_not.B: Sepsis can cause both disorders, but the metabolic acidosis usually dominates; here the respiratory alkalosis dominates and lactate is normal.
why_not.C: Pulmonary embolism causes respiratory alkalosis but does not explain an anion gap acidosis with a normal lactate.
why_not.D: An osmolar gap points to a toxic alcohol, which does not produce this dominant primary respiratory alkalosis.
why_not.E: Hyperthyroidism can increase ventilation but does not explain an anion gap metabolic acidosis with a normal lactate.

questions.pearl: A dominant respiratory alkalosis with an anion gap metabolic acidosis should make you think of salicylate poisoning; check a salicylate level.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 1: ABG Interpretation — Dr. Rachel Givelber, 7/23/2026 (slide 7; transcript excerpts 01_P014, 01_P015, 01_P016)

questions.topic: Post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis
questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man with severe COPD who uses home oxygen undergoes emergency laparotomy for a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. An arterial blood gas obtained 2 months ago at a pulmonary clinic visit, when he was at his baseline, showed pH 7.35, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L. He remains intubated after surgery, with the ventilator set to a respiratory rate of 20/min and a tidal volume of 450 mL. He takes no diuretics, has not vomited, has no nasogastric tube, and has received only 0.9% saline, with no blood products or bicarbonate. Blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg. Laboratory results 2 hours after surgery are shown.
TestResult
Sodium139 mEq/L
Potassium4.0 mEq/L
Chloride97 mEq/L
Bicarbonate32 mEq/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Arterial pH7.53
Arterial PCO240 mm Hg
Arterial PO2 (FiO2 0.40)92 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's alkalemia?
questions.explanation: His baseline gas (PaCO2 60, bicarbonate 32) reflects chronic hypercapnia: in a chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys compensate over time, producing a compensatory metabolic alkalosis. After surgery he has been ventilated down to a normal PaCO2 of 40, but the bicarbonate is still 32, so the gas now looks like a primary metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.53). This post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis can fool you; it comes up most after an operation, when a chronically hypercapnic patient is ventilated to an end-tidal CO2 appropriate for someone else.

why_not.A: His bicarbonate was already 32 two months ago, before any surgical fluid shifts, and he takes no diuretics.
why_not.B: He has received only 0.9% saline, with no bicarbonate or blood products, so there is no alkali load.
why_not.D: Hyperaldosteronism causes a chloride-unresponsive alkalosis, typically with hypertension and hypokalemia; his potassium and blood pressure are normal.
why_not.E: He has not vomited and has no nasogastric drainage, so there is no gastric acid loss.

questions.pearl: When a chronically hypercapnic patient is ventilated to a 'normal' PCO2, the retained bicarbonate masquerades as a primary metabolic alkalosis.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 1: ABG Interpretation — Dr. Rachel Givelber, 7/23/2026 (transcript excerpts 01_P012, 01_P013)

questions.topic: Winter's formula and inadequate respiratory compensation
questions.stem:
A 46-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department after her partner found her difficult to arouse; an empty bottle of the partner's oxycodone is at the bedside. She is somnolent but protecting her airway. Respiratory rate is 12/min, blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg, and pulse is 112/min. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium134 mEq/L
Potassium5.2 mEq/L
Chloride98 mEq/L
Bicarbonate8 mEq/L
Glucose486 mg/dL
β-Hydroxybutyrate6.8 mmol/L
Albumin4.0 g/dL
Arterial pH7.08
Arterial PCO228 mm Hg
Arterial PO2 (room air)100 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid–base status?

options.A: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
options.B: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis
options.C: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis
options.D: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
options.E: Anion gap and non–anion gap metabolic acidosis

questions.explanation: The pH and PCO2 are both low; they moved in the same direction, so the primary process is a metabolic acidosis. Winter's formula predicts PaCO2 = 1.5 × 8 + 8 ± 2 = 18–22 mm Hg. Her PaCO2 of 28 is too high, so there is a coexisting respiratory acidosis, even though 28 is below 40. The anion gap is 134 − (98 + 8) = 28; its rise (16) equals the fall in bicarbonate (16), so there is no additional metabolic disorder.

why_not.A: Winter's formula predicts 18–22 mm Hg; a PaCO2 of 28 is inadequate compensation, not appropriate compensation.
why_not.C: A coexisting respiratory alkalosis would push the PaCO2 below 18–22 mm Hg, not above it.
why_not.D: The rise in the gap (16) equals the fall in bicarbonate (16), so no metabolic alkalosis is hidden.
why_not.E: Bicarbonate fell exactly as much as the gap rose, so there is no coexisting non-gap acidosis.

questions.pearl: In metabolic acidosis, a PaCO2 above the Winter's prediction means a coexisting respiratory acidosis, even when the PaCO2 is below 40.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 1: ABG Interpretation — Dr. Rachel Givelber, 7/23/2026 (slides 7, 8, 16, 42)

questions.topic: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation
questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of rapid palpitations and lightheadedness while playing basketball. He has no chest pain or dyspnea and takes no medications. He is alert and conversant. Temperature is 36.9 °C, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Lungs are clear. The 12-lead ECG shows an irregularly irregular tachycardia with ventricular rates varying from about 200 to 280/min; the QRS complexes are wide and change in width and shape from beat to beat. A screening ECG from a sports physical 1 year ago showed sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 100 ms, a slurred initial upstroke of the QRS complex in several leads, and a normal QTc.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic therapy?
questions.explanation: This is pre-excited atrial fibrillation: a fast, broad, and irregular rhythm in a patient whose prior sinus ECG showed pre-excitation, with a very short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS. Treating it like ordinary AF with drugs that slow the AV node lets impulses travel down the accessory pathway unrestricted and can precipitate VF. Procainamide is preferred because it acts directly on the accessory pathway.

why_not.A: Adenosine blocks the AV node, and it should not be given for an irregular wide-complex rhythm, where it can leave the accessory pathway conducting unrestricted.
why_not.B: A nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker slows the AV node and can allow unrestricted accessory-pathway conduction leading to VF.
why_not.C: Beta-blockade is standard AF rate control, but slowing the AV node in pre-excited AF can accelerate pathway conduction and provoke VF.
why_not.E: IV magnesium treats torsades (polymorphic VT with a long QT); his QTc was normal and his prior ECG shows pre-excitation instead.

questions.pearl: Fast, broad, irregular with prior pre-excitation = pre-excited AF: avoid AV-nodal blockers; procainamide is preferred.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 2: Acute Arrhythmia Management — Dr. Tanmay Gokhale, 7/10/2026 (slide 35; transcript excerpts 02_P024, 02_P025)
2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation

questions.topic: Torsades de pointes
questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman is hospitalized for community-acquired pneumonia and is receiving ceftriaxone and azithromycin. She has also received intravenous ondansetron for nausea and haloperidol for nocturnal delirium. On hospital day 3, telemetry records several self-terminating runs of a wide-complex tachycardia lasting 10 to 20 beats, in which the QRS amplitude and axis change continuously so that the complexes appear to twist around the baseline. Between runs she is awake and has no chest pain; blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg, and the rhythm is sinus at 62/min. A 12-lead ECG between runs shows a QTc of 590 ms; her QTc on admission was 450 ms. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Potassium3.4 mEq/L
Magnesium2.0 mg/dL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic therapy?
questions.explanation: Polymorphic VT occurring with a long QT is torsades de pointes. Any patient with torsades, sustained or nonsustained, belongs in an ICU, and the main treatment is IV magnesium, together with stopping QT-prolonging drugs such as ondansetron and antipsychotics. Beta-blockers are used for congenital long QT; in acquired long QT a faster heart rate is what helps shorten the QT, so slowing her rate would work against you.

why_not.A: Amiodarone is used for sustained monomorphic VT; torsades in the setting of a long QT is treated with IV magnesium.
why_not.C: Beta-blockers are used for congenital long QT; in acquired long QT a faster, not slower, heart rate helps shorten the QT.
why_not.D: Adenosine is considered only for regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia; this rhythm is polymorphic.
why_not.E: Procainamide is the agent for stable pre-excited AF, where it acts on the accessory pathway; it is not a treatment for torsades.

questions.pearl: Polymorphic VT plus a long QT = torsades: ICU, IV magnesium, and stop every QT-prolonging drug.

questions.topic: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman hospitalized for lower-extremity cellulitis reports palpitations on hospital day 2. She has hypertension but no known heart failure, arrhythmia, or stroke, and she takes no anticoagulant. She cannot say when the palpitations started. Heart rate is 136/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She is alert; lungs are clear, and there is no edema. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, narrow QRS complexes, and no delta waves. An echocardiogram 4 months ago showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Potassium4.1 mEq/L
Magnesium2.0 mg/dL
TSH1.8 mIU/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment of this arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: In a stable patient with AF, the goal is to slow the ventricular rate: start with an IV beta-blocker or a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem, which is appropriate here because her LVEF is normal (calcium channel blockers are avoided in HFrEF). Do not reach first for amiodarone: it can convert AF to sinus rhythm, which increases the risk of stroke in a patient who is not anticoagulated, so rate control without amiodarone is first-line whenever possible.

why_not.A: Amiodarone can convert AF to sinus rhythm, raising stroke risk when AF duration is unknown and she is not anticoagulated; keep it for when rate-control drugs can't be used.
why_not.B: Adenosine is used for regular narrow-complex SVT; an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia is AF, which is treated with rate control.
why_not.D: Procainamide is the drug of choice for pre-excited AF; her QRS complexes are narrow with no delta waves, so AV-nodal rate control is appropriate.
why_not.E: Electricity is for the unstable patient; she is stable, and restoring sinus rhythm without anticoagulation carries stroke risk.

questions.pearl: Stable AF with RVR: slow the rate first with an IV beta-blocker or diltiazem; don't reach first for amiodarone in a non-anticoagulated patient.

questions.topic: Asymptomatic Mobitz II AV block
questions.stem: A 77-year-old man is hospitalized for management of a severe gout flare of the knee. At 2 PM, while sitting in a chair talking with family, his telemetry shows sinus rhythm at 80/min with intermittent nonconducted P waves, about 1 of every 4 or 5 P waves. The PR interval of conducted beats is constant at 180 ms, including the beats immediately before and after each dropped QRS complex. The QRS duration is 130 ms with right bundle branch block morphology, and the ventricular rate is 60 to 64/min. He denies lightheadedness, chest pain, or syncope. Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He takes no beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker, or digoxin. Serum potassium and high-sensitivity troponin are normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Dropped QRS complexes with a fixed PR interval before and after the nonconducted P wave define second-degree Mobitz type II block. Even when it is asymptomatic, once reversible causes (beta-blockers, hyperkalemia, ischemia) are excluded, guidelines call for a pacemaker because the risk of progression to complete heart block is high, yet it is not an emergency: he does not need a pacemaker placed at 3 AM. The right step is to involve electrophysiology at the appropriate time to evaluate for a permanent pacemaker. Atropine works poorly at this level of block.

why_not.A: Atropine works best for sinus bradycardia or Mobitz I and poorly for Mobitz II, and he has no symptoms to treat.
why_not.B: Dopamine or epinephrine drips temporize symptomatic bradycardia; he is asymptomatic with a stable blood pressure.
why_not.C: Asymptomatic Mobitz II is not an emergency, so emergency temporary pacing is not needed.
why_not.D: Mobitz II carries a high risk of progressing to complete heart block, so a pacemaker is indicated even without symptoms.

questions.pearl: Asymptomatic Mobitz II needs a pacemaker (high risk of complete heart block), but it is not a 3 AM emergency.

questions.topic: Myocardial injury vs myocardial infarction
questions.stem:
A 74-year-old woman is in the intensive care unit with septic shock from obstructive pyelonephritis. After ureteral stent placement she remains on norepinephrine, with a mean arterial pressure of 67 mm Hg and a sinus heart rate of 108/min. She is alert and denies chest pain, chest pressure, or dyspnea. Her ECG is unchanged from 1 year ago, with no new ST-segment or T-wave changes and no Q waves. Bedside echocardiography shows normal left ventricular size and function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Serial high-sensitivity troponin T values are shown (99th-percentile upper reference limit for women, 14 ng/L).
Timehs-Troponin T
Day 1, 08:0046 ng/L
Day 1, 14:0078 ng/L
Day 2, 06:0061 ng/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate diagnosis for her troponin elevation?
questions.explanation: Myocardial injury is a troponin elevation that can be acute or chronic; rising and falling levels indicate acute injury, which does not necessarily mean infarction. Calling it an MI requires the troponin elevation plus at least one of: symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, or new loss of viable myocardium/new regional wall-motion abnormality. Sepsis and shock are among the non-MI causes of troponin elevation. She has none of the ischemic criteria, so the accurate diagnosis is acute myocardial injury, not a type 2 NSTEMI.

why_not.B: Her troponin values rise and then fall, which indicates acute rather than chronic injury.
why_not.C: Type 1 MI is plaque rupture or erosion with thrombus and, like any MI, requires evidence of ischemia, which is absent.
why_not.D: A supply-demand setting is not enough; type 2 MI still requires ischemic symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, or a new wall-motion abnormality.
why_not.E: Unstable angina describes new, rest, or crescendo angina; she has no anginal symptoms.

questions.pearl: Troponin elevation alone is myocardial injury; call it MI only with ischemic symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, or new wall-motion loss.

questions.topic: Posterior STEMI (STEMI equivalent)
questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia comes to the emergency department of a hospital with an on-site 24-hour cardiac catheterization laboratory because of 45 minutes of severe substernal pressure with diaphoresis. He chewed aspirin at home. Blood pressure is 144/86 mm Hg, heart rate 90/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air; lungs are clear. The 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with 2-mm horizontal ST-segment depression in V1 through V3, prominent R waves in V2 and V3, and upright T waves; there is no ST-segment elevation in any of the 12 standard leads. Posterior leads V7 through V9 are recorded and show 1-mm ST-segment elevation. His pain persists after sublingual nitroglycerin. The first high-sensitivity troponin result is pending.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Record right-sided leads V3R and V4R

questions.explanation: ST depression in V1 through V4 can be a posterior wall MI from circumflex or RCA occlusion; when you suspect it, record posterior leads V7 through V9. ST elevation there means the vessel is closed, so this is still a STEMI and needs emergency reperfusion. Planning angiography later is the approach for non-ST-elevation ACS, where immediate (primary) intervention is less necessary because the artery is usually at least partially patent; that reasoning does not apply to an occluded artery.

why_not.A: If any ECG shows a STEMI, that is a STEMI; reperfusion should not wait for a troponin result.
why_not.B: Right-sided leads look for right ventricular infarction; the posterior leads have already confirmed a posterior STEMI.
why_not.C: Delayed angiography is an approach for NSTE-ACS with a partially patent artery, not for an occluded vessel.
why_not.E: Noninvasive anatomic imaging only delays reperfusion of an artery that the ECG already shows is occluded.

questions.pearl: ST depression in V1-V3? Record V7-V9. Posterior ST elevation means a closed artery: it is a STEMI, so reperfuse emergently.

questions.topic: Early beta-blockers in ACS and cardiogenic shock risk
questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with an NSTEMI after 3 hours of chest pressure. She has received chewed aspirin, an unfractionated heparin infusion, and sublingual nitroglycerin, and coronary angiography is planned within 24 hours. Her chest pressure has largely resolved. Heart rate is 114/min (sinus tachycardia), blood pressure 106/68 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L/min of oxygen. Jugular venous pressure is 9 cm H2O, and there are bibasilar crackles one-third of the way up both lung fields. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with 1.5-mm horizontal ST-segment depression in V4 through V6. A colleague suggests starting metoprolol now to reduce myocardial oxygen demand.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to beta-blocker therapy at this time?
questions.explanation: In COMMIT/CCS-2, the reduction in reinfarction with early beta-blockade was counterbalanced by an increase in cardiogenic shock. Shock is more likely with age >70, HR >110, SBP <120 mm Hg, and rales, and she has all four. Beta-blockers should therefore not be used acutely in a patient at risk for shock; an oral beta-blocker can be started once she is hemodynamically stable.

why_not.B: IV beta-blockade in a patient at risk for shock is what increased cardiogenic shock in COMMIT.
why_not.C: Even an oral beta-blocker should not be started acutely while she has every marker of shock risk.
why_not.D: A titratable infusion is still acute beta-blockade in a patient at risk for cardiogenic shock.
why_not.E: Carvedilol is still a beta-blocker; starting it now carries the same shock risk.

questions.pearl: Before an early beta-blocker in ACS, check shock risk (age >70, HR >110, SBP <120, rales); if present, wait.

questions.topic: Glasgow-Blatchford score and disposition in upper GI bleeding
questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department after two episodes of black, tarry stool over the past day. He has taken ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 2 weeks for an ankle sprain. He has had no hematemesis, lightheadedness, or syncope. He has no history of liver disease, heart failure, or cancer and takes no other medications. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 84/min, without orthostatic changes. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Rectal examination shows black stool. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin14.2 g/dL
Platelet count245,000/µL
Blood urea nitrogen15 mg/dL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
INR1.0
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Admit for upper endoscopy within 24 hours
options.C: Admit to ICU for urgent upper endoscopy

questions.explanation: The Glasgow-Blatchford score combines BUN, hemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and cardiac failure, and it is most useful for the admission decision in the emergency department. This patient scores 1 (melena only), and a score ≤1 was 99% sensitive for ruling out a severe upper GI bleed. He also lacks early warning signs—hypotension, tachycardia, shock, hemoglobin below 8 g/dL or a 2-g/dL drop, cirrhosis, or malignancy—so discharge with outpatient endoscopy is appropriate.

why_not.B: With a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 1, a severe bleed is very unlikely and admission is not needed.
why_not.C: He has no hypotension, tachycardia, shock, or hemoglobin drop that would justify ICU care.
why_not.D: CT angiography localizes active, brisk bleeding; he is hemodynamically normal with melena.
why_not.E: High-dose IV PPI infusion is for bleeding ulcers with high-risk stigmata after endoscopic therapy, not very-low-risk patients.

questions.pearl: A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 1 or less identifies very-low-risk upper GI bleeding that can be managed as an outpatient.

questions.topic: Pre-endoscopic prokinetic in active upper GI bleeding
questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man is hospitalized after two episodes of hematemesis of bright red blood over the past 4 hours. He takes naproxen daily for osteoarthritis. He has no history of liver disease, and there are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. On arrival, blood pressure was 92/58 mm Hg and pulse rate was 116/min. After 2 L of crystalloid through two large-bore intravenous lines and 2 units of red blood cells, blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 96/min. A bolus of intravenous pantoprazole has been given, and upper endoscopy is planned within the next 2 hours. He vomited fresh red blood again 30 minutes ago. Laboratory results after transfusion are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin8.4 g/dL
Platelet count262,000/µL
INR1.1
Blood urea nitrogen44 mg/dL
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional therapy before endoscopy?

options.D: Red cell transfusion to hemoglobin >10 g/dL

questions.explanation: With active bleeding, blood in the stomach obscures the endoscopic view, so a prokinetic is given before EGD to move blood out of the stomach and improve visualization. IV erythromycin (3 mg/kg—around 250 mg—given 20–120 minutes before EGD) produced an empty stomach in 69% vs 37% of patients, with less need for a second endoscopy, fewer transfusions, and shorter length of stay. Octreotide, which reduces splanchnic flow, is for patients with cirrhosis or suspected liver-related bleeding—not this patient with an NSAID-associated bleed.

why_not.A: Octreotide is for cirrhosis or suspected liver-related (variceal) bleeding, which he does not have.
why_not.B: PPIs are more effective than histamine-2 receptor antagonists, and he is already receiving a PPI.
why_not.C: His platelet count is well above the transfusion goal of 50,000/µL.
why_not.D: Liberal transfusion has not improved outcomes and may cause harm; his hemoglobin is already above the transfusion threshold.

questions.pearl: Active upper GI bleeding with blood in the stomach: give IV erythromycin before EGD to clear the view.

questions.topic: PPI regimen after endoscopic therapy for a bleeding ulcer
questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman was hospitalized 3 days ago with melena and hypotension. Upper endoscopy showed a 1.5-cm duodenal bulb ulcer with active oozing, which was treated with epinephrine injection and hemoclips. She has since received high-dose intravenous pantoprazole. She has had no further bleeding, her hemoglobin level has been stable for 48 hours, and she is tolerating a regular diet. Gastric biopsies for Helicobacter pylori are pending, and she has stopped taking ibuprofen. She is ready for discharge.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate acid-suppressive regimen at discharge?

options.A: Oral PPI once daily for 8 weeks
options.B: Oral PPI twice daily for 2 weeks, then daily
options.C: Oral famotidine twice daily for 8 weeks
options.D: Oral PPI twice daily for 3 days, then stop

questions.explanation: For bleeding ulcers with high-risk stigmata treated endoscopically, give high-dose PPI for 3 days—a bolus plus continuous infusion, or intermittent IV twice-daily dosing, which gives similar outcomes. Then continue oral PPI twice daily through the first 2 weeks, followed by once daily. This patient's actively oozing ulcer was treated endoscopically and she has completed 3 days of IV therapy, so she is due for the twice-daily oral phase. PPIs are more beneficial than histamine-2 receptor antagonists such as famotidine.

why_not.A: Once-daily dosing follows only after the first 2 weeks of twice-daily therapy for an endoscopically treated high-risk ulcer.
why_not.C: PPIs are more beneficial than histamine-2 receptor antagonists for bleeding ulcers.
why_not.D: Twice-daily therapy should continue through the first 2 weeks, and acid suppression should not then be stopped.
why_not.E: A recently treated high-risk ulcer still requires PPI therapy after discharge.

questions.pearl: After endoscopic therapy of a high-risk ulcer: 3 days of high-dose IV PPI, then oral PPI twice daily through the first 2 weeks, then daily.

questions.topic: Localizing brisk lower GI bleeding
questions.stem:
A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after passing large amounts of bright red and maroon blood per rectum beginning 2 hours ago, without abdominal pain. She has known sigmoid diverticulosis. She takes amlodipine and does not take antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, or NSAIDs. On arrival, blood pressure is 86/52 mm Hg and pulse rate is 118/min. After 2 L of crystalloid and 2 units of red blood cells through large-bore intravenous lines, blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg and pulse rate is 102/min, but she continues to pass red blood. A nasogastric aspirate returns bilious fluid without blood. Laboratory results on arrival are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin8.1 g/dL (12.6 g/dL one month ago)
Platelet count210,000/µL
INR1.0
Blood urea nitrogen17 mg/dL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Painless, large-volume hematochezia in an older adult is typical of diverticular bleeding, which is arterial and can be brisk. CT angiography is the next step: it is fast and localizes the bleeding source well, and a positive study directs interventional radiology to the bleeding vessel for embolization. A tagged red blood cell scan is less specific and slower, and colonoscopy cannot be done without a bowel preparation—the colon is full of stool and blood—no matter how brisk the bleeding.

why_not.A: Colonoscopy requires a bowel preparation; without one the colon is full of stool and blood.
why_not.B: A tagged red blood cell scan is less specific and slower than CT angiography.
why_not.D: Capsule endoscopy evaluates the small bowel for obscure bleeding, not brisk colonic hemorrhage.
why_not.E: Surgery is a last resort for refractory bleeding; the source should first be localized for targeted therapy.

questions.pearl: Brisk painless hematochezia: after resuscitation, CT angiography localizes the source for embolization—not a tagged RBC scan or unprepped colonoscopy.

questions.topic: Hypoxemia with a normal A–a difference
questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman is evaluated for 3 months of progressive dyspnea. She describes fatigue that worsens toward the end of each day and new difficulty swallowing. She lives near sea level and has not traveled recently. Temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate is 94/min, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 24/min with shallow respirations, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Lung examination is normal. Chest radiograph is clear, transthoracic echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function, and hemoglobin is 13.1 g/dL. Arterial blood gas results obtained while she breathes room air are shown.
TestResult
pH7.32
PaCO266 mm Hg
PaO260 mm Hg
Bicarbonate33 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's hypoxemia?
questions.explanation: Because she is breathing room air, the FiO2 is known and the A–a difference can be calculated: PAO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) − 66/0.8 ≈ 67 mm Hg, so her A–a difference is only about 7 mm Hg—normal. Hypoxemia with a normal A–a difference has two causes: high altitude or hypoventilation. She lives near sea level, and her high PaCO2 with a compensatory rise in bicarbonate points to chronic hypoventilation. End-of-day fatigue and dysphagia should raise concern for myasthenia gravis as the cause.

why_not.B: Diffusion impairment (e.g., fibrosis or emphysema) widens the A–a difference, which is normal here.
why_not.C: Low inspired oxygen also gives a normal A–a difference, but she lives near sea level and her high PaCO2 points to hypoventilation.
why_not.D: A right-to-left shunt produces an elevated A–a difference, which she does not have.
why_not.E: V/Q mismatch elevates the A–a difference, and her chest radiograph is clear.

questions.pearl: Hypoxemia with a normal A–a difference means hypoventilation or altitude; calculate A–a only when FiO2 is known, as on room air or when intubated.

questions.topic: Shunt: hypoxemia refractory to oxygen
questions.stem:
A 36-year-old woman with influenza A pneumonia is intubated for worsening hypoxemic respiratory failure. Chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral alveolar opacities. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function, and an agitated-saline study shows no intracardiac shunt. The ventilator is set to volume control with an FiO2 of 1.0 and PEEP of 12 cm H2O. Temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate is 116/min, blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 88%. Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL. Arterial blood gas results are shown.
TestResult
pH7.34
PaCO246 mm Hg
PaO258 mm Hg
Bicarbonate24 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why her hypoxemia persists despite an FiO2 of 1.0?
questions.explanation: Because she is intubated, her FiO2 is known: on 100% oxygen her alveolar PO2 is roughly 650 mm Hg, yet her PaO2 is 58—a markedly elevated A–a difference, which places her in the V/Q mismatch, shunt, and diffusion group rather than hypoventilation or altitude. Severe pneumonia and ARDS cause V/Q mismatch plus physiologic shunt: blood flows past alveoli filled with inflammatory material and returns to the left heart unchanged. The special feature of shunt is that it cannot be fixed by giving more oxygen, so hypoxemia that persists on an FiO2 of 1.0 points to shunt.

why_not.A: Her PaCO2 is near normal and the A–a difference is markedly widened, so hypoventilation cannot explain this degree of hypoxemia.
why_not.B: Diffusion impairment (thickened membranes or lost surface area) is not what makes hypoxemia persist on 100% oxygen; that is the hallmark of shunt.
why_not.C: She is receiving an FiO2 of 1.0, so inspired oxygen tension is high, not low.
why_not.D: Low V/Q units are present in ARDS, but V/Q mismatch improves with supplemental oxygen; persistence on an FiO2 of 1.0 points to shunt.

questions.pearl: Hypoxemia that does not correct with more oxygen points to shunt—classically physiologic shunt from severe pneumonia or ARDS.

questions.topic: Pulse oximetry error and occult hypoxemia
questions.stem:
A 64-year-old Black woman with a dark complexion who is hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia is receiving oxygen 3 L/min by nasal cannula, and her pulse oximeter has read 93% to 95% for several hours. Because she reports increasing dyspnea, an arterial blood gas is drawn while the oximeter reads 94%; a new sensor placed on a different finger also reads 94%. The plethysmographic waveform is crisp and tracks the cardiac monitor, her hands are warm with brisk capillary refill, and she is not wearing nail polish. Co-oximetry results from the arterial sample are shown.
TestResult
Arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2)86%
PaO252 mm Hg
Carboxyhemoglobin1.2%
Methemoglobin0.7%
Hemoglobin12.4 g/dL
questions.question: Which of the following best explains the difference between the pulse oximeter reading and the measured arterial saturation?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximeters were developed and tested largely in light-skinned volunteers and can overestimate saturation in patients with darker skin. In a study of paired oximetry and arterial blood gas readings, occult hypoxemia—low arterial saturation that the oximeter missed—was found in about 11.7% of readings from Black patients versus 3.6% of readings from White patients. The other common sources of error—faulty equipment, inadequate perfusion, nail polish, and other hemoglobins—have each been excluded here. More invasive testing (an arterial blood gas) is sometimes needed when the oximeter reading does not fit the patient.

why_not.A: Carboxyhemoglobin is 1.2%, so carbon monoxide does not explain the gap.
why_not.B: Methemoglobin is 0.7%, so an abnormal hemoglobin is not responsible.
why_not.C: Warm hands, brisk capillary refill, and a crisp waveform that tracks the pulse indicate adequate perfusion.
why_not.E: A new sensor on another finger gives the same reading, so equipment failure is unlikely.

questions.pearl: Pulse oximetry can miss hypoxemia, more often with darker skin; when the reading does not fit the patient, check a blood gas.

questions.topic: Suspected PE: start LMWH before imaging
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began 3 days after a 14-hour flight. His right calf is swollen and tender. He takes no medications and has no history of bleeding. Temperature is 37.1 °C, heart rate is 112/min, blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Lungs are clear. CT pulmonary angiography is ordered, but the scanner will not be available for about 4 hours. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin14.6 g/dL
Platelet count236,000/µL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
High-sensitivity troponin T31 ng/L (reference <14)
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Withhold anticoagulation until CT confirms the diagnosis
options.B: Start an intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion
options.D: Obtain an echocardiogram before starting anticoagulation

questions.explanation: Anticoagulation is the first treatment for PE. When PE is strongly suspected—here, signs of leg DVT and tachycardia after a long flight, with an elevated troponin—bleeding risk is low, and imaging is delayed, therapeutic anticoagulation should start before the diagnosis is confirmed. LMWH is preferred over unfractionated heparin: a weight-based injection reaches therapeutic anticoagulation much faster than a heparin drip, which can leave patients subtherapeutic for much of the first day. The preference for LMWH holds even for patients who may later need advanced therapies.

why_not.A: Waiting 4 hours leaves a high-probability, low-bleeding-risk patient untreated; anticoagulation should begin while imaging is pending.
why_not.B: A heparin infusion takes much longer to reach therapeutic levels than LMWH and is not the preferred agent.
why_not.D: Most patients do not need a stat echocardiogram, and it should not delay anticoagulation.
why_not.E: PE is not yet confirmed, and systemic thrombolysis is reserved mainly for hemodynamic instability; he is normotensive.

questions.pearl: Strongly suspected PE, low bleeding risk, delayed scan? Give LMWH now—before imaging—even if advanced therapy might follow.

questions.topic: PE risk stratification: normotensive shock
questions.stem:
A 63-year-old man with acute pulmonary embolism is admitted from the emergency department on therapeutic enoxaparin. He is alert and oriented, and his urine output is adequate. Temperature is 37.0 °C, heart rate is 104/min, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 93% on oxygen 2 L/min by nasal cannula. CT pulmonary angiography shows a saddle embolus extending into both main pulmonary arteries, with a right ventricle–to–left ventricle diameter ratio of 1.4. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
High-sensitivity troponin T78 ng/L (reference <14)
BNP640 pg/mL
Lactate3.4 mmol/L
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following findings indicates that this normotensive patient has incipient cardiopulmonary failure (normotensive shock)?

options.A: Saddle embolus on CT pulmonary angiography
options.E: Need for supplemental oxygen at 2 L/min

questions.explanation: PE risk stratification now looks beyond a single blood pressure. RV dilation and an elevated troponin signal RV strain and myocardial injury (Category C features), not shock. Markers of organ hypoperfusion despite normal blood pressure—lactate >2, acute kidney injury, altered mental status—define normotensive shock, a pre-cardiopulmonary failure state (Category D) with higher risk of death and decompensation, in which advanced therapies can be considered. Here, lactate is the only hypoperfusion marker. Clot size alone does not define risk: clot burden has not been shown to correlate with mortality.

why_not.A: A saddle embolus reflects clot burden, which alone does not define risk or indicate hypoperfusion.
why_not.C: RV dilation reflects RV strain (a Category C feature), not systemic hypoperfusion.
why_not.D: Troponin elevation reflects myocardial injury and supports Category C, but it is not a marker of hypoperfusion.
why_not.E: Oxygen need is captured by the new respiratory modifier, not by the definition of normotensive shock.

questions.pearl: Normal blood pressure is not reassurance in PE: lactate >2, AKI, or altered mentation signal normotensive shock (Category D).

questions.topic: Normotensive PE with RV strain: avoid systemic thrombolysis
questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man with COPD is admitted with acute pulmonary embolism. CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral lobar and segmental emboli with a right ventricle–to–left ventricle diameter ratio of 1.3. He is receiving therapeutic enoxaparin, is alert, and his symptoms have not worsened since arrival. Temperature is 37.0 °C, heart rate is 96/min, blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. A colleague proposes systemic thrombolytic therapy because of the RV dilation and troponin elevation. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
High-sensitivity troponin T48 ng/L (reference <14)
Lactate1.3 mmol/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours with anticoagulation
options.C: Switch to an intravenous heparin infusion
options.D: Continue enoxaparin and consult the PE response team

questions.explanation: This normotensive patient has RV dilation and an elevated troponin without hypoperfusion. When systemic lysis was tested in such patients (PEITHO), deaths were few and similar in both groups; the benefit came from less hemodynamic decompensation, at the cost of about 5-fold more major bleeding and 12-fold more stroke, including intracranial hemorrhage. Guidelines therefore do not recommend routine systemic thrombolysis in normotensive patients like him; it is reserved mainly for hemodynamic instability (Category E). He should stay hospitalized on LMWH with close monitoring, and the PE response team should be involved, as recommended for Categories C through E.

why_not.A: Patients with RV dysfunction and elevated biomarkers belong in the hospital, not on outpatient therapy.
why_not.B: In stable patients like him, systemic lysis prevented decompensation without lowering mortality and caused more major bleeding and stroke.
why_not.C: LMWH is preferred over a heparin drip, even when escalation to advanced therapy is possible.
why_not.E: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for situations such as failed or contraindicated thrombolysis, clot-in-transit, or PFO—none present here.

questions.pearl: RV strain plus troponin with normal blood pressure: continue LMWH, monitor closely, involve the PE response team; reserve systemic lysis for hemodynamic instability.

questions.topic: Sepsis masquerading as alcohol withdrawal
questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder was admitted 2 days ago for alcohol withdrawal; his last drink was 4 days ago. His previous withdrawal episodes began within 24 hours of stopping alcohol and included tonic-clonic seizures. Despite several doses of intravenous lorazepam, he remains confused, and his withdrawal-scale scores are high. Overnight he developed profuse diarrhea and abdominal pain. Temperature is 38.9 °C, heart rate is 128/min (sinus tachycardia), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 30/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on oxygen 2 L/min. He is flushed and diaphoretic and is oriented only to self. Extremities are warm with brisk capillary refill. The abdomen is diffusely tender without peritoneal signs. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Leukocyte count19,800/µL with 14% bands
Lactate3.6 mmol/L
Creatinine1.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9)
Glucose214 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.C: CT of the abdomen first, then antibiotics if positive
options.E: Blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics now

questions.explanation: Sepsis can masquerade as or coexist with alcohol withdrawal, intoxication, or dehydration. This patient is febrile, tachycardic, and tachypneic with leukocytosis and bandemia, has a likely abdominal source, and shows early organ dysfunction—confusion and acute kidney injury. When sepsis is probable, give antibiotics immediately; obtain blood cultures first when possible, but do not delay antibiotics to get them. Withdrawal treatment can continue in parallel, but escalating sedation alone would leave a life-threatening infection untreated.

why_not.A: Phenobarbital may help refractory withdrawal, but it does not treat the probable sepsis driving his fever, lactate, and kidney injury.
why_not.B: More benzodiazepine will not treat the infection driving his fever, confusion, and organ dysfunction.
why_not.C: Imaging to find the source is reasonable, but antibiotics for probable sepsis should not wait for the scan.
why_not.D: Sedation does not address the probable sepsis explaining his fever, elevated lactate, and acute kidney injury.

questions.pearl: Fever, confusion, and organ dysfunction during 'withdrawal'? Think sepsis—culture and give antibiotics immediately rather than only escalating sedation.

questions.topic: Septic shock: urgent source control of an obstructed kidney
questions.stem:
A 67-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department for 2 days of right flank pain, fever, and rigors. Temperature is 39.2 °C, heart rate is 118/min, blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 24/min. She has right costovertebral angle tenderness. After 30 mL/kg of crystalloid she remains hypotensive, and norepinephrine is started, raising her mean arterial pressure to 67 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Blood and urine cultures were obtained, and piperacillin-tazobactam was given 1 hour ago. CT shows an 8-mm obstructing stone at the right ureterovesical junction with moderate hydronephrosis and perinephric stranding. It is 11 PM, and the on-call team proposes ureteral stent placement as the first case tomorrow morning. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Leukocyte count21,400/µL
Lactate4.2 mmol/L
Creatinine1.8 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Broaden antibiotics to meropenem and keep the morning stent plan
options.B: Arrange emergent decompression of the right kidney tonight
options.C: Start tamsulosin to promote stone passage
options.D: Add vancomycin and keep the morning stent plan
options.E: Repeat CT in 48 hours if fever persists

questions.explanation: Antibiotics are already running, but an obstructing stone with hydronephrosis means the infection has not been source-controlled—a commonly missed opportunity. When a septic patient has a source that needs drainage, obtain urgent surgical or IR consultation; achieving source control within about 6 hours is associated with lower mortality than delayed control. In septic shock this cannot wait until morning, so the obstructed kidney should be decompressed tonight, even if that means paging colleagues in the middle of the night.

why_not.A: Broader coverage does not drain an obstructed, infected kidney, and delaying source control in septic shock worsens outcomes.
why_not.C: Waiting for stone passage leaves an infected, obstructed collecting system undrained in a patient in shock.
why_not.D: Adding antibiotics does not substitute for timely source control.
why_not.E: The source is already identified; the problem is delayed drainage, not diagnosis.

questions.pearl: Septic shock with a drainable source—such as an obstructed infected kidney—needs source control within hours, not tomorrow morning.

questions.topic: Predicting fluid responsiveness in sepsis
questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia and sepsis-induced hypoperfusion has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 2 hours, along with antibiotics. He is breathing spontaneously and is in sinus rhythm. Heart rate is 112/min, blood pressure is 90/52 mm Hg (mean arterial pressure 65 mm Hg), and respiratory rate is 26/min. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Lactate has fallen from 4.1 to 3.2 mmol/L. Bedside ultrasound shows normal left ventricular systolic function. The team is deciding whether to give more intravenous fluid.
questions.question: Which of the following is the best way to predict whether additional fluid will increase his cardiac output?

options.A: Central venous pressure via a new central line
options.B: Inferior vena cava diameter on bedside ultrasound
options.C: Passive leg raise with LVOT VTI measurement
options.D: Blood pressure response to the first 30 mL/kg bolus
options.E: Jugular venous pressure on physical examination

questions.explanation: A passive leg raise—moving the patient from 45° head-up with legs flat to head flat with legs raised to 45°—returns about a unit of pooled blood to the heart: a volume challenge without giving extra volume. If stroke volume rises (for example, LVOT VTI on bedside ultrasound), more fluid is likely to increase cardiac output. Historical parameters—CVP and IVC size—are not reliable predictors of volume responsiveness on their own, and the blood-pressure response to fluid already given does not tell you what the next bolus will do.

why_not.A: CVP is a static pressure that does not predict volume responsiveness.
why_not.B: IVC size is unreliable as a single variable and should not stand alone to decide on more fluid.
why_not.D: A response to fluid already given does not tell you what the next liter will do.
why_not.E: JVP is a bedside estimate of CVP and shares its inability to predict fluid responsiveness.

questions.pearl: To know whether fluid will help, test with a passive leg raise and measure stroke volume—not CVP or IVC size alone.

questions.topic: Creatinine rise without a fall in GFR
questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection began dolutegravir-lamivudine 4 weeks ago; hepatitis B surface antigen was negative. He feels well and takes no other medications or supplements. He has had no vomiting, diarrhea, NSAID use, or contrast exposure. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Laboratory results are shown.
TestBefore therapyWeek 4
Creatinine0.92 mg/dL1.06 mg/dL
Blood urea nitrogen13 mg/dL13 mg/dL
Potassium4.2 mEq/L4.3 mEq/L
UrinalysisNo protein, blood, leukocytes, or crystalsNo protein, blood, leukocytes, or crystals
questions.question: Which of the following best explains the change in serum creatinine?
questions.explanation: Creatinine is filtered at the glomerulus and also secreted by the tubule. A drug that blocks tubular creatinine secretion raises serum creatinine and looks like a fall in GFR, but it is actually reduced secretion. Drugs that do this include trimethoprim, cimetidine, and antiretrovirals such as dolutegravir. His small rise (0.92 to 1.06 mg/dL over 4 weeks) does not meet the AKI definition, a rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or to 1.5 times baseline within a week, and his BUN and urinalysis are unchanged.

why_not.A: AIN typically produces pyuria or white cell casts and a progressive rise; his urinalysis is normal and the change is small.
why_not.C: Nothing suggests reduced kidney perfusion (no volume loss, NSAIDs, or hypotension), and BUN is unchanged.
why_not.D: Assay interference comes from substances such as cefoxitin, flucytosine, or acetoacetate, not dolutegravir.
why_not.E: Crystal-induced obstruction occurs with drugs such as high-dose IV acyclovir; his urinalysis shows no crystals.

questions.pearl: A small creatinine rise after trimethoprim, cimetidine, or dolutegravir may reflect blocked tubular secretion, not a fall in GFR.

questions.topic: Postrenal AKI above the bladder
questions.stem:
A 76-year-old man with prostate cancer metastatic to bone and pelvic lymph nodes is hospitalized for pain control. An indwelling urinary catheter was placed on admission for urinary retention and drains clear urine; a bladder scan after flushing the catheter shows 20 mL. Over 3 days, his serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.8 mg/dL, with urine output of about 600 mL/day. He has taken no NSAIDs and received no contrast. Blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg; mucous membranes are moist and there is no edema. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Blood urea nitrogen62 mg/dL
Creatinine2.8 mg/dL
Potassium4.9 mEq/L
Bicarbonate22 mEq/L
Urinalysis3–5 RBCs/hpf; no WBCs or casts
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Not all obstruction is below the bladder: a working urinary catheter excludes only lower-tract obstruction. His catheter drains and his bladder is empty, yet creatinine keeps rising, and prostate or bladder cancer can obstruct the ureters above the bladder. Obstruction is diagnosed by imaging, usually ultrasonography or CT, and with high suspicion you should go beyond ultrasound if needed. Urine chemistries are variable in obstruction and will not settle the question.

why_not.A: The catheter drains and the bladder is empty, so any obstruction must be above the bladder.
why_not.B: He shows no sign of volume depletion, and fluid will not relieve ureteral obstruction.
why_not.C: Urine chemistries are variable in obstruction and cannot establish or exclude it.
why_not.E: Biopsy is premature before obstruction, a reversible cause, has been excluded by imaging.

questions.pearl: A working Foley excludes only lower-tract obstruction; pelvic cancers can block the ureters, so image the kidneys.

questions.topic: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis
questions.stem:
A 67-year-old woman is evaluated for a serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL found on routine testing; it was 0.9 mg/dL 4 months ago. Omeprazole was started 8 weeks ago for dyspepsia; she has taken amlodipine and atorvastatin for years. She reports mild fatigue but no fever, rash, NSAID use, or contrast exposure. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg, and she appears euvolemic. Kidney ultrasonography shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Blood urea nitrogen30 mg/dL
Creatinine2.6 mg/dL
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Bicarbonate20 mEq/L
Blood eosinophils2%
Urine protein (dipstick)1+
Urine microscopy10–20 WBCs/hpf, 3–5 RBCs/hpf, WBC casts, no bacteria
Urine cultureNo growth
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: A rising creatinine with white cell casts and a sterile urine culture points to acute interstitial nephritis, and proton pump inhibitors are among the drugs most often responsible. The classic triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia is rarely seen, so its absence should not reassure you. Everyone agrees on the first step: discontinue the offending drug. Whether to add glucocorticoids is the controversy, not the starting point.

why_not.B: Urine eosinophils have poor sensitivity and specificity for AIN and would not change the next step.
why_not.C: Glucocorticoids are controversial in AIN; they may be used if kidney function does not improve after the drug is stopped, but they are not the first step.
why_not.D: White cell casts with a sterile culture indicate interstitial nephritis, not pyelonephritis.
why_not.E: She is euvolemic with a BUN-to-creatinine ratio near 12:1 and an active sediment, which argue against prerenal AKI.

questions.pearl: Suspected drug-induced AIN: stop the culprit first; the classic fever, rash, and eosinophilia triad is rarely seen.

questions.topic: Indications for dialysis in AKI
questions.stem:
A 63-year-old man is in the ICU on day 8 of oliguric acute tubular necrosis that followed septic shock; vasopressors were stopped 4 days ago. Today he reports sharp chest pain that improves when he sits forward. Temperature is 37.0°C, blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg, pulse is 96/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. A pericardial friction rub is heard; the lungs are clear and there is no edema. An ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression. Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion without tamponade. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Blood urea nitrogen96 mg/dL
Creatinine7.1 mg/dL
Potassium5.0 mEq/L
Bicarbonate19 mEq/L
Phosphorus6.4 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Established acute tubular necrosis has no specific pharmacologic treatment. Care is supportive, and you dialyze when an indication appears; one of those indications is the uremic syndrome, whose manifestations include pericarditis. This patient has developed uremic pericarditis during oliguric ATN, which is an indication for dialysis by itself, even though his potassium, bicarbonate, and volume status do not require it.

why_not.A: NSAIDs can worsen AKI, and anti-inflammatory drugs do not remove the uremic toxins driving the pericarditis.
why_not.B: Glucocorticoids do not treat uremia; dialysis does.
why_not.C: There is no tamponade, so drainage is not indicated.
why_not.D: Diuretics treat volume overload, which he does not have, and do not treat uremic pericarditis.

questions.pearl: Uremic pericarditis or encephalopathy in AKI is an indication for dialysis, even when potassium, bicarbonate, and volume are controlled.

questions.topic: Code status: making a recommendation
questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with non-small cell lung cancer metastatic to bone, who uses home oxygen, is admitted with pneumonia, sepsis, and acute kidney injury. He is receiving intravenous antibiotics and 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula, and over the past 2 months he has spent most of each day in a chair. He is alert and has decision-making capacity. He knows his cancer cannot be cured and says a good day means being at home with his wife and grandchildren. He has no advance directive and has never discussed CPR with a physician. With his permission, the resident explains that for patients with similar health conditions, there is a very low chance that CPR and life support would help him recover enough to return home and live as he does now. After hearing that some people would accept those efforts despite the low chance while others would prefer a natural death, he says, "If my chances of getting home are that low, I wouldn't want to go through all that. But I want to keep treating this pneumonia."
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Keep him full code until his wife can decide
options.B: Recommend comfort-focused care and stop antibiotics
options.C: Ask him to accept or decline each resuscitation procedure
options.D: Recommend no CPR while continuing current treatments
options.E: Request an ethics consultation before changing his code status

questions.explanation: This is the last step of the C-P-R framework: check for prior advance care planning, provide prognosis and assess preferences, then make a recommendation that accounts for his prognosis and his preferences given that prognosis. Metastatic malignancy and acute critical illness predict a poor outcome after cardiac arrest. Pair the recommendation with reassurance—"we're going to keep doing all the medical treatments with the goal of you getting better"—and if his heart stops despite that, allow a natural death rather than CPR or life support. A no-CPR recommendation does not mean stopping antibiotics.

why_not.A: He has decision-making capacity and has stated his preference, so the decision is his to make now rather than his wife's.
why_not.B: He wants to keep treating the pneumonia; a no-CPR recommendation is paired with continuing all treatments aimed at getting better.
why_not.C: A procedure-by-procedure menu focuses on interventions rather than his goals, the pattern that makes typical code status discussions ineffective.
why_not.E: There is no conflict to resolve; his prognosis and clearly stated values already support a clear recommendation.

questions.pearl: After giving prognosis and hearing preferences, make a recommendation—and pair "no CPR" with continued full treatment aimed at getting better.

questions.topic: Code status: responding to "just do everything"
questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on 3 L/min of home oxygen, heart failure, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease is admitted with pneumonia. She uses a wheelchair outside her home and needs help with bathing. She is alert and has decision-making capacity, and her daughter is at the bedside. Her record contains no advance directive or prior code status discussion. After asking permission, the resident explains that for patients with similar health conditions, there is a low chance that CPR and life support would help her recover enough to return home. She crosses her arms and replies firmly, "Just do everything."
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next response?

options.A: Document full code status and end the discussion
options.B: Explore the concerns behind her request
options.C: Tell her CPR is futile and will not be offered
options.D: Restate the survival statistics in more detail
options.E: Ask her daughter to decide on code status

questions.explanation: "Just do everything" is a statement to explore, not a final answer. Approach it like a differential diagnosis with cognitive, emotional, and spiritual possibilities: a sense of abandonment or fear of death, incomplete understanding, or a need to be sure she will still receive the best medical care possible. Because it is most often rooted in emotion or identity, start there—respond with curiosity about what she means and what lies behind the request, rather than recording "full code" and leaving the room.

why_not.A: Treating the statement as the end of the conversation ("full code, I'm out") misses the fears or misunderstandings that often drive it.
why_not.C: Her values may favor CPR despite low odds; the task is to understand her request, not to shut the conversation down.
why_not.D: Repeating numbers addresses only a possible knowledge gap, whereas the statement most often comes from emotion or identity—explore first.
why_not.E: She has capacity and has not asked to defer; turning to a surrogate is for patients who prefer that someone else discuss it.

questions.pearl: "Just do everything" is a symptom, not a decision: build a differential (emotional, cognitive, spiritual) and explore before documenting full code.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 10: Code Status — Dr. Jane Schell, 7/8/2026 (slide 27; transcript excerpt 10_P026)
Quill TE, Arnold R, Back AL. Discussing treatment preferences with patients who want 'everything', Ann Intern Med 2009

questions.topic: DKA with low potassium: replete before insulin
questions.stem:
A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is evaluated in the emergency department for 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He stopped taking his insulin because he was unable to eat. He is alert and oriented. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg, pulse rate is 116/min, and respiration rate is 28/min with deep, rapid breathing. Mucous membranes are dry, and the abdomen is mildly tender without guarding. A 1-L bolus of 0.9% saline has been started. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium132 mEq/L
Potassium3.1 mEq/L
Chloride96 mEq/L
Bicarbonate11 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen26 mg/dL
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL
Glucose486 mg/dL
Phosphorus3.4 mg/dL
β-Hydroxybutyrate5.2 mmol/L
Venous pH7.18
Venous Pco230 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: In DKA, potassium shifts out of cells (insulin deficiency, hyperosmolarity) and is then lost in the urine, so a value that is already low on presentation means substantial potassium has been lost. Insulin moves glucose and potassium into cells, so serum potassium will fall further once insulin starts. The rule: if the initial potassium is low, get potassium into the patient before starting insulin. Bicarbonate is not needed here; it may be beneficial only when pH is below about 6.9–7.0.

why_not.A: Insulin started now would drive potassium into cells and worsen the hypokalemia; potassium comes first.
why_not.C: Bicarbonate is not needed at pH 7.18; it may help only when pH is below about 6.9–7.0.
why_not.D: Phosphorus is normal; IV phosphate is reserved for severe hypophosphatemia (<1 mg/dL).
why_not.E: He is still volume depleted, and his glucose-corrected sodium (about 138 mEq/L) is not high, so isotonic saline should continue.

questions.pearl: In DKA, check potassium before insulin: if it is low, give potassium first—insulin will drive it lower.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 13: Diabetic Ketoacidosis — Dr. Margaret Zupa, 6/30/2026 (slides 27, 30)
Umpierrez GE et al. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report, Diabetes Care 2024

questions.topic: Euglycemic DKA with an SGLT2 inhibitor
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is evaluated in the emergency department for 2 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and malaise. Four days ago she underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy and has eaten very little since. Her medications are metformin and empagliflozin, which she resumed after surgery. She is alert. Blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg, pulse rate is 110/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. Mucous membranes are dry, and the surgical incisions are clean. Intravenous 0.9% saline has been started. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium136 mEq/L
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Chloride102 mEq/L
Bicarbonate10 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen24 mg/dL
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Glucose184 mg/dL
β-Hydroxybutyrate5.8 mmol/L
Lactate1.3 mmol/L
Venous pH7.19
Venous Pco227 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Saline alone until glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL

questions.explanation: This is euglycemic DKA: glucose below 200–250 mg/dL with an elevated anion gap, low bicarbonate, and low pH (β-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L). Its incidence is rising with SGLT2 inhibitor use. Treatment is exactly the same as for any DKA—fluids, electrolytes, and an insulin infusion—except that, because glucose is already below 250 mg/dL, dextrose-containing fluid is started up front alongside the insulin. A near-normal glucose is not a reason to withhold insulin.

why_not.A: Withholding insulin because glucose is near normal leaves the ketoacidosis untreated.
why_not.B: Bicarbonate is not indicated at pH 7.19; it is considered only below about 6.9–7.0.
why_not.C: Correction-scale insulin alone does not treat ketoacidosis in a vomiting patient; she needs a DKA insulin protocol.
why_not.D: Potassium is 4.6 mEq/L, so potassium is added to the fluids without delaying insulin.

questions.pearl: Ketoacidosis with glucose under 250 mg/dL on an SGLT2 inhibitor is still DKA: give insulin and start dextrose up front.

questions.topic: Insulin pump removed during surgery in type 1 diabetes
questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with a 20-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is hospitalized for open reduction and internal fixation of a wrist fracture. She uses an insulin pump filled with insulin lispro and a continuous glucose monitor, and she managed her pump herself before surgery. The pump was disconnected and removed in the operating room. At 6 PM she returns to the surgical floor drowsy from general anesthesia and opioids and is unable to manage her pump; she will not eat until morning. No insulin has been given since the pump was removed. Vital signs are normal. Point-of-care glucose is 196 mg/dL.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate insulin management at this time?

options.B: Hold insulin until she resumes eating
options.D: Reconnect the pump tomorrow when alert
options.E: Recheck glucose and ketones in the morning

questions.explanation: Insulin pumps deliver only rapid-acting insulin (such as lispro or aspart), never long-acting insulin. Once the pump comes off, a person with type 1 diabetes has no basal insulin on board and is at risk for DKA much faster than someone taking long-acting insulin; a pump removed in the operating room and never replaced with subcutaneous insulin is a classic route to DKA. She cannot run her pump, so she needs subcutaneous basal insulin right away. Holding insulin, or using a sliding scale alone without basal coverage, invites DKA.

why_not.A: Correction insulin alone provides no basal coverage, so ketoacidosis can still develop.
why_not.B: People with type 1 diabetes need basal insulin even when not eating; holding it invites DKA.
why_not.D: Waiting until morning leaves her with no insulin overnight—the typical route from pump removal to DKA.
why_not.E: Waiting for ketones to appear delays treatment she needs now; give basal insulin.

questions.pearl: Pumps contain no long-acting insulin—when a pump comes off in type 1 diabetes, give basal insulin right away.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 13: Diabetic Ketoacidosis — Dr. Margaret Zupa, 6/30/2026 (slides 48, 53; transcript excerpt 13_P007)

questions.topic: Hyperchloremic acidosis after DKA treatment and transition to subcutaneous insulin
questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus was admitted to the intensive care unit 20 hours ago with diabetic ketoacidosis after missing insulin doses (initial venous pH 7.06, bicarbonate 6 mEq/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 7.4 mmol/L). He has been treated with an intravenous insulin infusion, about 7 L of 0.9% saline, and dextrose-containing fluids once glucose fell. He has not received any subcutaneous insulin. His nausea has resolved, and he is asking for breakfast. His home regimen is insulin glargine 22 units daily plus insulin lispro with meals. Current laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium140 mEq/L
Potassium4.2 mEq/L
Chloride114 mEq/L
Bicarbonate19 mEq/L
Glucose168 mg/dL
β-Hydroxybutyrate0.3 mmol/L
Venous pH7.32
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Continue insulin infusion until bicarbonate is normal
options.C: Stop infusion now, then start subcutaneous insulin at lunch
options.D: Start subcutaneous insulin, then stop infusion in 2 hours
options.E: Stop infusion now, then use correction-scale insulin only

questions.explanation: His DKA has resolved: pH and bicarbonate are normal or close to normal, glucose is under 200 mg/dL, and he is ready to eat. The remaining mild acidosis has a normal anion gap with high chloride—a non–anion gap (expansion) acidosis from large volumes of IV fluid. It is common after successful DKA treatment and, if mistaken for persistent DKA, needlessly delays the switch to subcutaneous insulin. Because IV insulin is gone within minutes of stopping, overlap subcutaneous insulin with the drip by 2 hours.

why_not.A: The low bicarbonate reflects saline-related hyperchloremia, not ketoacidosis; waiting for it to normalize needlessly prolongs the drip.
why_not.B: Bicarbonate therapy is reserved for severe acidosis (pH below about 6.9–7.0); his pH is 7.32.
why_not.C: IV insulin is gone within minutes, so stopping without an overlap risks rebound hyperglycemia and recurrent DKA.
why_not.E: Correction-scale insulin without basal coverage is a recognized cause of DKA recurrence after transition.

questions.pearl: After DKA treatment, a normal–anion gap hyperchloremic acidosis is not persistent DKA—transition, overlapping subcutaneous insulin with the drip by 2 hours.

questions.topic: Initial vasoactive agent in hypotensive cardiogenic shock
questions.stem:
A 63-year-old man with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 15%) is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of worsening dyspnea, early satiety, and new confusion. Blood pressure is 74/50 mm Hg (mean arterial pressure 58 mm Hg), heart rate is 114/min, respiratory rate is 28/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula. The jugular venous pressure is elevated, there are bibasilar crackles, and the extremities are cool and mottled. Bedside echocardiography shows a severely dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle without pericardial effusion. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Lactate5.4 mmol/L
Creatinine2.5 mg/dL (baseline 1.1)
Alanine aminotransferase520 U/L
Sodium127 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial vasoactive agent?
questions.explanation: He is hypotensive and hypoperfused. In the lecture's head-to-head "cage match," norepinephrine wins: compared with norepinephrine, dopamine caused more arrhythmia, more GI reactions, and lower survival, and in a randomized trial of infarct-related shock epinephrine led to more refractory shock. Phenylephrine should not be used in cardiogenic shock, because raising afterload without adding contractility leaves a failing ventricle in worse shape. Milrinone is rarely an initial drug. Norepinephrine is therefore the reasonable first agent.

why_not.A: Compared with norepinephrine, dopamine caused more arrhythmias and GI reactions and lower survival.
why_not.B: In a randomized trial of infarct-related shock, epinephrine led to more refractory shock than norepinephrine.
why_not.C: An inodilator that worsens hypotension and arrhythmia; it is rarely an initial agent in a patient this hypotensive.
why_not.E: A pure vasoconstrictor raises afterload without adding contractility, further lowering output from a failing ventricle.

questions.pearl: Hypotensive cardiogenic shock: start norepinephrine; avoid phenylephrine (afterload without contractility); dopamine and epinephrine fared worse than norepinephrine head-to-head.

questions.topic: Hemodynamic profile of normotensive cardiogenic shock
questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 15%) is admitted with 5 days of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, early satiety, and new confusion. Blood pressure is 112/96 mm Hg, heart rate is 118/min, respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on 4 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. The jugular venous pulse is visible at the angle of the jaw with the patient upright, there are crackles over both lung bases, and the extremities are cool and mottled. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated, severely hypokinetic left ventricle and no pericardial effusion. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Lactate4.6 mmol/L
Creatinine2.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.0)
Alanine aminotransferase410 U/L
Sodium128 mEq/L
Chloride94 mEq/L
Bicarbonate18 mEq/L

A pulmonary artery catheter is placed.
questions.question: Which of the following sets of hemodynamic values is most likely? (CI in L/min/m²; PCWP and CVP in mm Hg; SVR in dyn·s/cm⁵)
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock classically combines high filling pressures, high SVR, and low cardiac output. Jugular venous distension means a high right atrial pressure, and orthopnea with basilar crackles means high left-sided pressure backing up into the lungs. Her blood pressure is preserved only because low output triggered a catecholamine surge and vasoconstriction; the small stroke volume and high SVR produce her narrow pulse pressure. The elevated lactate, kidney injury, and liver injury show hypoperfusion despite a normal-looking blood pressure.

why_not.A: High output with low SVR and low filling pressures is a vasodilatory pattern, not a cold, congested patient with a failing ventricle.
why_not.C: With this low output, an SVR of 750 could not sustain a mean pressure near 100 mm Hg; vasoplegia is a late, ominous stage of cardiogenic shock.
why_not.D: Isolated right-sided failure would not explain orthopnea and crackles; her severely dysfunctional left ventricle raises the wedge pressure.
why_not.E: A high-output, vasodilated profile would give warm extremities and a wide pulse pressure, not her cool, mottled skin and narrow pulse pressure.

questions.pearl: A 'normal' blood pressure with a narrow pulse pressure can hide cardiogenic shock: low output, high filling pressures, and compensatory high SVR.
