questions.topic: Right ventricular failure unmasked on left-sided temporary MCS
questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man with an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock underwent primary PCI of the proximal left anterior descending artery and placement of an Impella CP (a left ventricular microaxial flow pump) 6 hours ago. He remains hypotensive, with a mean arterial pressure of 60 mm Hg on norepinephrine 0.15 mcg/kg/min and dobutamine 5 mcg/kg/min, and urine output is 10 mL/h. Echocardiography shows the pump correctly positioned, a small underfilled left ventricle, and no pericardial effusion. Pulmonary artery catheter and laboratory data are shown.
TestResult
Right atrial pressure21 mm Hg
Pulmonary artery pressure28/14 mm Hg
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure11 mm Hg
Cardiac index1.6 L/min/m²
Lactate, 4 hours ago3.0 mmol/L
Lactate, now5.6 mmol/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Increase the Impella CP performance level
options.B: Exchange the Impella CP for an Impella 5.5

questions.explanation: The PA catheter shows which side is failing. Here the right atrial pressure (21) exceeds the wedge (11) with a low cardiac index and rising lactate: the left ventricle is decompressed and underfilled because the right ventricle is failing. As the lecture put it, in RV failure a left-sided device "doesn't help them"; the fix is right-sided support (for example, an Impella RP Flex or ProtekDuo), which refills the left ventricle. These numbers come from the PA catheter, hence the lecture's rule: use a PA catheter with MCS.

why_not.A: More left-sided pump speed cannot help when the failing right ventricle is not delivering blood to an already underfilled left ventricle.
why_not.B: A larger left-sided pump still leaves the failing right ventricle unsupported.
why_not.C: A balloon pump is another left-sided afterload device and does not support the right ventricle.
why_not.D: With a right atrial pressure of 21 mm Hg the right ventricle is already congested; more volume would worsen RV distension.

questions.pearl: On a left-sided device, CVP above wedge with low output means RV failure — add right-sided support; check both sides with a PA catheter.

questions.topic: Temporary MCS with a survival benefit in STEMI-related shock
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction after 3 hours of chest pain. He is awake and following commands and has not had a cardiac arrest. Blood pressure is 84/60 mm Hg on norepinephrine 0.1 mcg/kg/min, heart rate is 112/min, and the extremities are cool. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. Echocardiography shows an LVEF of 25%, a normal-sized right ventricle, and no mechanical complication. He undergoes emergency PCI of an occluded proximal left anterior descending artery. Right heart catheterization results are shown.
TestResult
Right atrial pressure9 mm Hg
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure27 mm Hg
Cardiac index1.8 L/min/m²
questions.question: In addition to revascularization, which of the following is most likely to improve his survival?
questions.explanation: This is STEMI-related cardiogenic shock with left-sided congestion (high wedge, normal right atrial pressure) in an awake patient. DanGer Shock, the only randomized trial of temporary mechanical support to show a mortality benefit in STEMI shock, tested the Impella CP, a microaxial flow pump, and lowered mortality with a number needed to treat of 8. The benefit came at a price: more bleeding, limb ischemia, sepsis, and dialysis, with a number needed to harm of 6 for the composite safety end point, so careful selection and complication surveillance matter.

why_not.A: Balloon pumps have not shown a survival benefit in randomized trials; DanGer Shock is the only positive trial of temporary support in STEMI shock.
why_not.B: Venoarterial ECMO has not reduced mortality in randomized trials of infarct-related shock.
why_not.D: His hemodynamics show left-sided, not right-sided, failure: the wedge pressure is high and the right atrial pressure is normal.
why_not.E: Standard care without a microaxial pump was the control arm in DanGer Shock and had higher mortality; escalating pressors is itself linked to higher mortality.

questions.pearl: In selected STEMI shock, a microaxial flow pump (DanGer Shock) lowers mortality (NNT 8) but adds complications (NNH 6): bleeding, limb ischemia, dialysis.

questions.topic: Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment
questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man is admitted with 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and low-grade fevers, with a 6-kg weight loss. He has not seen a physician in several years, takes no medications, and has no drug allergies. Temperature is 38.1 °C, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on ambient air, falling to 85% with ambulation. He has oral thrush, and fine crackles are heard bilaterally. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody testing is reactive; CD4 count and HIV RNA are pending. Bronchoscopy is planned for tomorrow. Results are shown.
TestResult
Arterial pH (ambient air)7.46
PaCO232 mm Hg
PaO262 mm Hg
Bicarbonate22 mEq/L
Lactate dehydrogenase540 U/L
1,3-β-D-glucan480 pg/mL (reference: below 60)
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: This picture—subacute dyspnea and dry cough, thrush, hypoxemia, diffuse interstitial infiltrates, a high LDH, and an elevated (though nonspecific) β-D-glucan in untreated HIV—is Pneumocystis pneumonia. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is the preferred drug; primaquine plus clindamycin is for patients who are truly TMP-SMX allergic, and atovaquone, an outpatient option, is not for severe disease. Because his PaO2 is less than 70 mm Hg, corticosteroids are added, given as a standardized 21-day taper.

why_not.A: Atovaquone is an outpatient option that is not used for severe disease, and he also needs adjunctive corticosteroids.
why_not.B: Atovaquone is not appropriate for severe disease, and nothing here precludes the preferred drug, TMP-SMX.
why_not.C: Primaquine plus clindamycin is reserved for true TMP-SMX allergy, and this regimen omits the corticosteroids he needs.
why_not.E: TMP-SMX is the right antimicrobial, but a PaO2 below 70 mm Hg also calls for adjunctive corticosteroids.

questions.pearl: Suspected PJP: TMP-SMX is preferred; add corticosteroids when PaO2 is below 70 mm Hg, as a 21-day taper.

questions.topic: Timing of ART with opportunistic infections
questions.stem: A 36-year-old man is hospitalized and newly diagnosed with HIV. His CD4 count is 38/µL, and his HIV-1 RNA is 310,000 copies/mL. He has never taken antiretroviral therapy (ART). Treatment for an opportunistic infection has been started, and the team plans to begin bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine; resistance testing has been sent.
questions.question: For which of the following opportunistic infections should the start of ART be deferred for several weeks?
questions.explanation: ART timing depends on the opportunistic infection. In cryptococcal and TB meningitis, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can be life-threatening, so ART is delayed until the meningitis is under control—often several weeks into treatment. When there is no treatment for the infection other than immune reconstitution, as in PML, cryptosporidiosis, and microsporidiosis, ART starts immediately. For other opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis pneumonia or disseminated MAC, ART starts when feasible—almost always within 2 weeks.

why_not.A: Cryptosporidiosis has no effective treatment other than immune reconstitution, so ART should start immediately.
why_not.C: For disseminated MAC, ART should start as soon as feasible rather than being deferred for weeks.
why_not.D: For Pneumocystis pneumonia, ART should start within 2 weeks of beginning treatment.
why_not.E: PML has no treatment other than immune reconstitution, so ART should start immediately.

questions.pearl: Defer ART several weeks for cryptococcal or TB meningitis (IRIS risk); start immediately for PML or cryptosporidiosis; otherwise generally within 2 weeks.

questions.topic: Acute HIV infection
questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man returns to discuss HIV test results. His last HIV test, 1 year ago, was negative, and he has never taken HIV preexposure or postexposure prophylaxis. He feels well today but had a flu-like illness last week with fever, headache, myalgias, and fatigue. He is afebrile, and small lymph nodes are palpable in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions. Results of laboratory HIV testing are shown.
TestResult
HIV-1 p24 antigenReactive
HIV-1/HIV-2 antibodiesNonreactive
HIV-1 RNA (PCR)480,000 copies/mL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Oral fluid rapid HIV antibody test
options.D: Await genotype and HLA-B*5701 results before starting ART

questions.explanation: A reactive p24 antigen with nonreactive antibodies and a very high HIV RNA is acute HIV infection—the interval between detectable HIV RNA and the appearance of anti-HIV antibodies, when RNA is always detectable and p24 antigen is usually positive. Treatment should start right away, without waiting for antibodies to appear. Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine is the go-to regimen for new diagnoses and can be started the same day without waiting for test results: integrase resistance is rare, and unlike abacavir-containing regimens, it requires no HLA-B*5701 testing.

why_not.A: The reactive p24 antigen and high HIV RNA already indicate acute HIV; waiting for antibodies to appear only delays treatment.
why_not.B: Point-of-care tests are less sensitive, and an antibody-only test will be negative before seroconversion.
why_not.C: An antibody-based test will be negative before seroconversion, and the Western blot is no longer part of the diagnostic algorithm.
why_not.D: Same-day start is appropriate: integrase resistance is rare, and this regimen needs no HLA-B*5701 testing.

questions.pearl: Reactive p24 antigen, negative antibodies, high HIV RNA = acute HIV: start bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine the same day without awaiting results.

questions.topic: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes
questions.stem:
A 71-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and stage 4 chronic kidney disease is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of generalized weakness. Medications are lisinopril, spironolactone, carvedilol, and furosemide. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse is 58/min. He is placed on a cardiac monitor. An ECG shows peaked T waves, flattened P waves, and a QRS duration of 150 ms. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Potassium7.4 mEq/L
Sodium136 mEq/L
Bicarbonate20 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen64 mg/dL
Creatinine3.4 mg/dL
Glucose132 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.explanation: Weakness with hyperkalemic ECG changes makes this a hyperkalemic emergency. With the patient on a monitor, the first drug is IV calcium gluconate, which stabilizes the cardiac membrane; its effect begins within 3–5 minutes and lasts 30–60 minutes. Calcium does nothing to lower the potassium, so it must be followed promptly by therapy that does, starting with insulin and glucose to drive potassium back into cells.

why_not.A: Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into cells but does not protect the myocardium; give it right after calcium.
why_not.B: Potassium binders remove potassium over hours and do not address the immediate cardiac toxicity.
why_not.C: Bicarbonate mainly helps when metabolic acidosis is significant, and it does not stabilize the cardiac membrane.
why_not.E: Inhaled beta-2 agonists are an adjunct for shifting potassium, not a substitute for calcium when the ECG is abnormal.

questions.pearl: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: put the patient on a monitor and give IV calcium gluconate first; it protects the heart but does not lower potassium.

questions.topic: Drug-induced hyperkalemia: trimethoprim
questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man with hypertension and stage 3a chronic kidney disease is seen 6 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for acute bacterial prostatitis. He has taken lisinopril at the same dose for 3 years, and his potassium was 4.6 mEq/L last month. He takes no NSAIDs, beta-blockers, or potassium supplements and does not have diabetes. Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg. An ECG is normal. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Potassium6.1 mEq/L
Sodium138 mEq/L
Bicarbonate22 mEq/L
Creatinine1.5 mg/dL (baseline 1.4 mg/dL)
Estimated GFR49 mL/min/1.73 m2
Glucose104 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following best explains the recent increase in this patient's serum potassium?

options.A: Inhibition of renin release from the kidney
options.C: Blockade of the epithelial sodium channel
options.D: Reduced GFR limiting renal potassium excretion
options.E: Insulin deficiency limiting cellular potassium uptake

questions.explanation: Final urinary potassium excretion is set in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron. Trimethoprim acts like amiloride and triamterene: it blocks the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) there, and TMP-SMX is a big cause of hyperkalemia. His lisinopril dose is unchanged, his eGFR is essentially stable, and renal potassium excretion is not significantly affected until GFR falls below 15–20 mL/min, so stage 3a CKD does not explain the new rise. In any hyperkalemic patient, ask which drugs are causing it.

why_not.A: Impaired renin release (from NSAIDs, beta-blockers, diabetes, or older age) is absent or long-standing here and cannot explain a rise that began after the antibiotic.
why_not.B: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism is how spironolactone and eplerenone raise potassium, not trimethoprim.
why_not.D: Potassium excretion is preserved until GFR falls below about 15–20 mL/min; his eGFR is 49 and stable.
why_not.E: He does not have diabetes and his glucose is normal; the new factor is the antibiotic.

questions.pearl: New hyperkalemia on TMP-SMX: trimethoprim blocks ENaC like amiloride and is a major cause of drug-induced hyperkalemia.

questions.topic: Pseudohyperkalemia
questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia is sent to the emergency department because a routine serum potassium was 6.6 mEq/L. She feels well and has no weakness. She takes no medications that affect potassium, and her kidney function is normal. Blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg and pulse is 74/min. An ECG is normal. A repeat sample, drawn without a tourniquet or fist clenching, is not hemolyzed. Results from the repeat sample are shown.
TestResult
Potassium (serum)6.4 mEq/L
Sodium139 mEq/L
Bicarbonate25 mEq/L
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Glucose96 mg/dL
Leukocyte count184,000/µL
Hemoglobin11.2 g/dL
Platelet count148,000/µL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Intravenous calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring
options.C: Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate three times daily
options.D: Urgent hemodialysis via a temporary catheter
options.E: Whole-blood potassium on a blood gas analyzer

questions.explanation: Before treating emergent hyperkalemia, verify that the potassium is accurate: consider hemolysis, fist clenching, and pseudohyperkalemia, which should be considered when the white cell count is very high. She has no symptoms, a normal ECG, and no identifiable cause for true hyperkalemia. Fragile leukemic cells can break down in the sample after it is drawn, creating an artifact that makes the potassium read higher than it really is. Check a whole-blood potassium on a blood gas analyzer.

why_not.A: Calcium is given for ECG changes from hyperkalemia; her ECG is normal and the value may be an artifact.
why_not.B: Insulin drives potassium into cells and could cause hypokalemia if her true potassium is normal.
why_not.C: A binder would remove potassium she may not have in excess; confirm the value first.
why_not.D: Dialysis is for true, refractory hyperkalemia, which has not been established.

questions.pearl: Hyperkalemia with a normal ECG, no risk factors, and marked leukocytosis: confirm with a whole-blood potassium before treating.

questions.topic: Hypokalemia with metabolic acidosis
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman who had a total colectomy with end ileostomy 3 weeks ago is admitted with 4 days of high ileostomy output (about 2.5 L/day), fatigue, and leg weakness. Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg and pulse is 104/min. Proximal leg strength is 4/5 bilaterally. An ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium134 mEq/L
Potassium2.6 mEq/L
Chloride112 mEq/L
Bicarbonate13 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen30 mg/dL
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL)
Magnesium2.0 mg/dL
Glucose92 mg/dL
Albumin3.6 g/dL
questions.question: Which of the following should be given first?
questions.explanation: High ileostomy output increases potassium loss and, through volume depletion, induces secondary hyperaldosteronism with urinary potassium losses. She now has symptomatic hypokalemia with a metabolic acidosis (anion gap 134 − [112 + 13] = 9). Replete potassium first: giving bicarbonate shifts potassium into cells and can drive an already low potassium dangerously lower. Check magnesium and replete it as needed; hers is normal, so it is not the priority. Treat the acidosis after potassium is restored.

why_not.B: Bicarbonate shifts potassium into cells and could worsen severe hypokalemia; give it after potassium is repleted.
why_not.C: Magnesium should be repleted when low, but her magnesium is normal.
why_not.D: Dextrose stimulates insulin release, which drives potassium into cells and would lower it further.
why_not.E: Spironolactone does not treat severe symptomatic hypokalemia; she needs potassium now.

questions.pearl: Hypokalemia plus metabolic acidosis: replete potassium first, because bicarbonate shifts potassium into cells and can make it dangerously low.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 16: Hyperkalemia — Dr. Cary Boyd Shiwarski, 7/16/2026 (slides 10, 25; transcript excerpt 16_P027)

questions.topic: Hypotonic hyponatremia with a normal measured osmolality
questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department after being found confused at home among many empty beer cans. He takes no medications. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. He has slurred speech and mild scleral icterus; there is no ascites or edema. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium115 mEq/L
Potassium3.4 mEq/L
Chloride80 mEq/L
Bicarbonate24 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen6 mg/dL
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Glucose82 mg/dL
Ethanol230 mg/dL
Serum osmolality (measured)288 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality72 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium11 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hyponatremia?

options.D: Low solute intake with excess water intake
options.E: Low effective arterial blood volume from cirrhosis

questions.explanation: A normal measured osmolality does not mean normal tonicity. Urea and ethanol are ineffective osmoles: they raise osmolality but not tonicity. Subtracting them (288 − 6/2.8 − 230/4.6 ≈ 236 mOsm/kg) reveals hypotonic hyponatremia. A urine osmolality below 100 means the kidneys are excreting maximally dilute urine and vasopressin is absent, which rules out vasopressin-mediated causes such as SIAD and low effective arterial volume. This is beer potomania: heavy beer drinking with little food.

why_not.A: Pseudohyponatremia requires high lipids or proteins; ethanol explains the normal osmolality, and true tonicity is low.
why_not.B: Ethanol distributes throughout total body water, so it is an ineffective osmole and cannot cause hypertonic hyponatremia.
why_not.C: SIAD is vasopressin-mediated, with a urine osmolality of 100 or more; his urine is maximally dilute at 72.
why_not.E: Low effective arterial volume stimulates vasopressin, so the urine osmolality would be 100 or more, not 72.

questions.pearl: Normal osmolality is not normal tonicity: subtract urea and ethanol. Urine osmolality <100 means no vasopressin; think beer potomania.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 17: Hyponatremia — Dr. Herbert Rondon-Berrios, 7/31/2026 (slides 9, 11, 15; transcript excerpt 17_P011)
2014 ESE/ESICM/ERBP Clinical Practice Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Hyponatraemia

questions.topic: Urine sodium versus urine chloride in hyponatremia
questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease has had 6 days of vomiting undigested food after meals. He takes no medications. Blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg supine and pulse is 110/min. A succussion splash is present. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium127 mEq/L
Potassium3.1 mEq/L
Chloride84 mEq/L
Bicarbonate32 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen34 mg/dL
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Glucose96 mg/dL
Serum osmolality270 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality520 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium46 mEq/L
Urine chloride<10 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hyponatremia?
questions.explanation: A urine osmolality of 520 in hypotonic hyponatremia shows that vasopressin is present. A urine sodium of 30 or more usually means the kidneys are not conserving sodium (normal or high effective arterial volume), but vomiting is an exception: it causes a metabolic alkalosis, and the kidneys excrete the excess bicarbonate as sodium bicarbonate, so urine sodium is high and unreliable. Urine chloride should be assessed instead; a value below 10 reveals low effective arterial blood volume, that is, hypovolemia.

why_not.A: SIAD requires a normal or high effective arterial volume; a urine chloride below 10 shows the kidneys are avidly conserving salt.
why_not.C: Aldosterone deficiency causes renal salt wasting, so urine chloride would be high, and alkalosis with hypokalemia would be unexpected.
why_not.D: He has no intracranial disease, and salt wasting would raise urine chloride along with urine sodium.
why_not.E: Primary polydipsia suppresses vasopressin, giving a urine osmolality below 100; his is 520.

questions.pearl: In hyponatremia with metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, judge volume status by the urine chloride, not the urine sodium.

questions.topic: Evaluation of suspected SIAD
questions.stem:
A 68-year-old woman with COPD is admitted after a ground-level fall. She has received three courses of oral prednisone for COPD exacerbations in the past 6 months, the most recent ending 2 weeks ago. Current medications are tiotropium and as-needed albuterol. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg without orthostatic change, and pulse is 82/min. She appears euvolemic. Head CT shows no acute abnormality. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium121 mEq/L
Potassium4.1 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen9 mg/dL
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Glucose94 mg/dL
Serum osmolality252 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality410 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium64 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
questions.explanation: Hypotonic hyponatremia with a urine osmolality of 100 or more and a urine sodium of 30 or more means vasopressin secretion is physiologically inappropriate: the differential is SIAD or cortisol deficiency. Secondary adrenal insufficiency mimics SIAD exactly; in a prospective study, 3.8% of patients first diagnosed with SIAD were reclassified as secondary adrenal insufficiency, more than half related to exogenous steroids. So, along with kidney function, order a morning cortisol before accepting SIAD, especially after repeated prednisone courses.

why_not.A: Vasopressin is elevated with cortisol deficiency too (and may even be undetectable in SIAD), so a level cannot exclude adrenal insufficiency.
why_not.B: Copeptin tracks vasopressin and likewise cannot distinguish SIAD from cortisol deficiency.
why_not.C: Her urine sodium already shows the kidneys are not sodium-avid; FENa adds nothing to exclude adrenal insufficiency.
why_not.D: A serum osmolality below 275 confirms hypotonic hyponatremia, so pseudohyponatremia need not be pursued.

questions.pearl: Before labeling hyponatremia SIAD, check a morning cortisol; secondary adrenal insufficiency mimics SIAD exactly.

questions.topic: Pseudohyponatremia
questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed IgG multiple myeloma is found to have a serum sodium of 126 mEq/L on a routine metabolic panel from the central laboratory. He has no confusion, headache, nausea, or gait change. He does not drink alcohol and has not received mannitol. Blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg, and he appears euvolemic. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Sodium126 mEq/L
Potassium4.4 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen18 mg/dL
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Glucose96 mg/dL
Total protein12.6 g/dL
Albumin3.0 g/dL
Serum osmolality (measured)286 mOsm/kg
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Intravenous bolus of 3% hypertonic saline solution
options.B: Fluid restriction to 1 liter per day
options.C: Whole-blood sodium on a blood gas analyzer

questions.explanation: First ask whether the hyponatremia is hypotonic. With a measured osmolality of 286, it could be hypertonic, hypotonic, or isotonic; his glucose and BUN are normal, and he has no ethanol or mannitol exposure. With a total protein of 12.6 g/dL from myeloma, the likely answer is pseudohyponatremia, a lab artifact of the indirect ion-selective electrodes used by automated analyzers when proteins or lipids are high. Confirm it with a whole-blood sodium on a blood gas analyzer, which should be normal.

why_not.A: Hypertonic saline treats symptomatic hypotonic hyponatremia; he is asymptomatic and may have no true hyponatremia.
why_not.B: Fluid restriction treats SIAD, but hypotonicity has not been established.
why_not.D: Cortisol testing belongs to the work-up of hypotonic, vasopressin-mediated hyponatremia, which is not established here.
why_not.E: He is euvolemic, and an artifactual sodium needs no correction.

questions.pearl: Hyponatremia with a normal measured osmolality and very high protein or lipids: confirm pseudohyponatremia with a whole-blood sodium on a blood gas analyzer.

questions.topic: C. difficile testing stewardship
questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is on postoperative day 3 after surgical repair of a hip fracture. She received cefazolin for 24 hours perioperatively. For opioid-associated constipation, senna and polyethylene glycol were started 2 days ago, and bisacodyl was added yesterday. Over the past 24 hours she has had 4 loose, nonbloody stools. She is afebrile with normal vital signs, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Leukocyte count is 8,200/µL. The overnight team ordered Clostridioides difficile testing, and the specimen has not yet been sent.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Send stool for glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin testing
options.D: Send stool for C. difficile PCR
options.E: Start loperamide and continue the bowel regimen

questions.explanation: C. difficile testing is meant for patients having three or more liquid stools in 24 hours without another explanation. Before testing, look for another cause—especially laxatives—and hold them for 48 hours if feasible. Her diarrhea began as her bowel regimen escalated, so stop the laxatives and reassess. Testing now risks detecting colonization, present in up to 20–25% of patients, and, most importantly, can delay diagnosis of the real cause of the diarrhea.

why_not.A: Testing while she is receiving laxatives risks detecting colonization and delaying the real diagnosis.
why_not.B: Empiric treatment is not indicated for laxative-associated diarrhea in an afebrile patient with a benign abdomen.
why_not.D: Any C. difficile test is premature while she is receiving laxatives; hold them for 48 hours first.
why_not.E: Loperamide treats the symptom while the cause—an escalating laxative regimen—continues.

questions.pearl: Test for C. difficile only with three or more unexplained liquid stools in 24 hours—hold laxatives for 48 hours first.

questions.topic: Asymptomatic bacteriuria and delirium
questions.stem:
An 82-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer dementia is brought from her assisted-living facility with 2 days of increased confusion and agitation. Her son reports that her urine has looked dark and smelled foul. Diphenhydramine was started for sleep 3 days ago. She cannot reliably describe her symptoms. Temperature is 37.0 °C, blood pressure 132/76 mm Hg, heart rate 82/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air. She is inattentive but in no distress. There is no suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness. A urine culture is pending. Results are shown.
TestResult
Leukocyte count7,600/µL
Sodium138 mEq/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Urine leukocyte esterasePositive
Urine nitritePositive
Urine microscopy30–50 WBC/hpf; many bacteria
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Withhold antibiotics and evaluate other causes
options.E: Repeat urine culture by straight catheterization

questions.explanation: Altered mental status alone is not a symptom of UTI, and dark, foul-smelling, or cloudy urine is not associated with UTI either. Without fever, localizing urinary findings, or signs of sepsis, her abnormal urinalysis most likely reflects asymptomatic bacteriuria. An infection severe enough to change brain function would be sepsis—infection causing organ dysfunction—which she does not have. Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults is associated with poor functional recovery, possibly because anchoring on the wrong diagnosis means missing the real problem, such as polypharmacy.

why_not.B: Without fever, localizing findings, or sepsis, ceftriaxone would only treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.
why_not.C: Nitrofurantoin would still treat asymptomatic bacteriuria and leave the cause of her delirium unaddressed.
why_not.D: Ciprofloxacin would treat asymptomatic bacteriuria and expose her to avoidable adverse effects.
why_not.E: A cleaner specimen would not change management; bacteriuria without urinary symptoms should not be treated.

questions.pearl: Confusion plus a positive urinalysis is not a UTI: without fever or urinary symptoms, withhold antibiotics and find the real cause.

questions.topic: Indwelling urinary catheter indications
questions.stem: A 74-year-old man is admitted to a medical floor with acute decompensated heart failure. He is receiving intravenous furosemide twice daily, with daily weights and intake and output recorded. He is alert, continent, and walks with a walker. Post-void residual volume on bladder scan is 40 mL. He asks for an indwelling urinary catheter so that he will not have to get up repeatedly to urinate, especially at night.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Place an indwelling catheter until diuresis is complete
options.B: Place an indwelling catheter for accurate output monitoring
options.C: Place an indwelling catheter and reassess its need daily
options.D: Perform intermittent straight catheterization every 6 hours
options.E: Offer an external urinary catheter instead

questions.explanation: Comfort measures at the end of life can justify a catheter, but a patient’s comfort or convenience otherwise does not: a patient wanting a Foley is not a reason to place one, and avoiding nighttime urination during twice-daily diuresis is not a good reason. For output monitoring, a catheter is appropriate when strict hourly monitoring in the intensive care unit is needed to titrate therapy; daily weights and intake and output on the floor do not qualify. Alternatives include intermittent straight catheterization or a male or female external drainage catheter—the reasonable, noninvasive option for a continent man who empties his bladder.

why_not.A: Avoiding nighttime urination during diuresis is not a valid indication for an indwelling catheter.
why_not.B: Intake-and-output monitoring on the floor does not qualify; that indication is for strict hourly monitoring in critically ill patients.
why_not.C: Daily reassessment matters, but there is no valid indication to place the catheter in the first place.
why_not.D: He voids normally with a low post-void residual, so repeated catheterization is unnecessary.

questions.pearl: A Foley is not for convenience—even during twice-daily diuresis; offer an external catheter instead.

questions.topic: When a CAC score of 0 does not justify deferring a statin
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man comes for a preventive visit. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. He has no diabetes, no known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and no family history of premature ASCVD, and he takes no medications. Blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and BMI is 28. His 10-year PREVENT-ASCVD risk is 6.7%. He is reluctant to start a statin, so coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is performed; the score is 0 Agatston units. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Total cholesterol212 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol42 mg/dL
Triglycerides130 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol (calculated)144 mg/dL
Hemoglobin A1c5.4%
eGFR88 mL/min/1.73 m²
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate lipid-lowering management?

options.A: Defer statin therapy and repeat CAC scoring in 3 to 7 years
options.B: Start statin therapy with an LDL-C goal <100 mg/dL
options.C: Start statin therapy with an LDL-C goal <55 mg/dL
options.E: Defer statin therapy and recalculate risk in 5 years

questions.explanation: A 10-year PREVENT-ASCVD risk of 6.7% is intermediate (5% to <10%), where LDL-lowering therapy should be considered after shared discussion, with an LDL-C goal <100 mg/dL. A CAC score of 0 allows deferral and repeat CAC in 3–7 years only when no high-risk features are present: no diabetes, familial hypercholesterolemia, tobacco use, family history of premature ASCVD, or LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL. Because he smokes, a zero score does not justify withholding a statin.

why_not.A: CAC-based deferral applies only when no high-risk features are present; his current tobacco use excludes him.
why_not.C: An LDL-C goal <55 mg/dL is reserved for very high-risk patients, such as those with ASCVD or a CAC score of at least 1000.
why_not.D: Statins remain first-line; nonstatin agents are add-ons when goals are not met on a statin.
why_not.E: Deferral ignores his intermediate risk and active smoking; statin therapy is indicated now.

questions.pearl: CAC = 0 permits deferring statins only without high-risk features — diabetes, FH, smoking, premature family history, or LDL-C ≥190.

questions.topic: LDL-C goal and next step in very-high-risk ASCVD
questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man is seen 4 months after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with PCI. He also had an ischemic stroke 3 years ago and has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He has taken atorvastatin 80 mg daily for more than 3 months, reports full adherence, and has no muscle symptoms. Lipoprotein(a) measured last year was 30 nmol/L. Fasting lipid results are shown.
TestResult
Total cholesterol132 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol40 mg/dL
Triglycerides120 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol68 mg/dL
Non-HDL cholesterol92 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in lipid management?

options.E: Measure apolipoprotein B before changing therapy

questions.explanation: With two or more major ASCVD events (a recent myocardial infarction and a prior ischemic stroke), he is at very high risk, with goals of LDL-C <55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL. His LDL-C of 68 and non-HDL-C of 92 mg/dL are above goal on a maximally tolerated statin. With the statin as the foundation, ezetimibe is the next add-on as goals require. Apolipoprotein B is used to assess residual risk once LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals have been met, not before.

why_not.A: LDL-C 68 and non-HDL-C 92 mg/dL exceed the very-high-risk goals of <55 and <85 mg/dL.
why_not.B: Fibrates are triglyceride-lowering agents; his triglycerides are normal and the gap is in LDL-C.
why_not.C: Omega-3 therapy targets elevated triglycerides in ASCVD; his triglycerides are 120 mg/dL.
why_not.E: Apolipoprotein B refines residual risk only after LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals are met, and his are not.

questions.pearl: Very-high-risk ASCVD: LDL-C <55 and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL; if above goal on a maximally tolerated statin, add ezetimibe.

questions.topic: Lipoprotein(a) as a risk enhancer in borderline primary-prevention risk
questions.stem:
A 60-year-old woman comes for a preventive visit. Her hypertension is controlled with amlodipine, and blood pressure today is 132/80 mm Hg. She does not smoke, has no diabetes or known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and has no family history of premature ASCVD. Her 10-year PREVENT-ASCVD risk is 4.0%. Lipoprotein(a), measured for the first time, is 212 nmol/L. After discussing her results, she says she would prefer to take a medication if it would lower her risk. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Total cholesterol222 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol54 mg/dL
Triglycerides110 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol (calculated)146 mg/dL
eGFR92 mL/min/1.73 m²
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Defer therapy until her 10-year risk reaches 5%
options.D: Start a PCSK9 inhibitor as initial therapy
options.E: Order genetic testing for familial hypercholesterolemia

questions.explanation: Her 10-year risk of 4.0% falls in the borderline-to-intermediate range (3% to <10%), where risk enhancers favor statin therapy. An Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L is a risk enhancer, associated with about a 1.4-fold higher ASCVD risk, so starting a statin is appropriate for a patient who wants treatment. Lp(a) should be measured at least once in all adults; because it is largely genetically determined and stable over a lifetime, repeat testing is generally not needed.

why_not.A: Lp(a) is largely genetic and stable over a lifetime; repeat testing is generally not needed.
why_not.B: Risk enhancers such as Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L favor treating borderline-risk patients now.
why_not.D: Statins are the foundation of LDL-C lowering; PCSK9 inhibitors are add-ons when goals are not met on a maximally tolerated statin.
why_not.E: An LDL-C of 146 mg/dL does not suggest familial hypercholesterolemia, and testing would not change the decision to start a statin.

questions.pearl: Check Lp(a) once in every adult; ≥125 nmol/L is a risk enhancer that favors a statin in borderline-to-intermediate risk — no need to repeat it.

questions.topic: POCUS: tamponade mistaken for pulmonary edema
questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is directly admitted from clinic for worsening dyspnea attributed to pulmonary edema, and intravenous furosemide has been ordered. On arrival, temperature is 37.6 °C, heart rate is 115/min, blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Chest radiograph shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Bedside ultrasound performed with her supervising attending shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion, collapse of the right ventricle in early diastole, a small hyperdynamic left ventricle, and a dilated inferior vena cava with minimal respiratory variation.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Give the ordered intravenous furosemide for pulmonary edema
options.C: Start a dobutamine infusion to augment contractility
options.E: Obtain CT pulmonary angiography before further treatment

questions.explanation: Clear lungs with an enlarged cardiac silhouette do not fit the sign-out of pulmonary edema. POCUS shows a large effusion with RV collapse in early diastole and a distended IVC, supporting cardiac tamponade. Tamponade is preload dependent, so the planned diuretic is the opposite of what she needs. The next step is to call cardiology right away for confirmation and urgent pericardiocentesis.

why_not.A: Diuresis reduces preload in a preload-dependent patient—the opposite of what tamponade requires.
why_not.B: Venodilation also lowers preload and can worsen tamponade physiology.
why_not.C: The problem is external compression of a hyperdynamic heart, not poor contractility; the effusion must be drained.
why_not.E: Delaying drainage for more imaging is inappropriate once a hemodynamically significant effusion explains her findings.

questions.pearl: Effusion with RV diastolic collapse and a plethoric IVC: think tamponade—hold diuretics and get cardiology for urgent pericardiocentesis.

questions.topic: Bedside compression ultrasound for DVT
questions.stem:
A 50-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer who is receiving chemotherapy is admitted at 10 PM with 3 days of painful swelling of the left leg. She has no history of bleeding. Temperature is 37.2 °C, heart rate is 92/min, blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The left calf is 4 cm larger in circumference than the right, with pitting edema. The vascular laboratory will not be available until the next morning. With a POCUS-credentialed attending supervising, the resident performs bedside compression ultrasonography; the left common femoral vein does not compress and contains echogenic material. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin11.8 g/dL
Platelet count210,000/µL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Begin anticoagulation and obtain a formal venous duplex
options.B: Begin anticoagulation; no formal study is needed
options.C: Withhold anticoagulation until the formal duplex result returns
options.D: Obtain a D-dimer level before deciding on treatment
options.E: Repeat bedside compression ultrasound in 24 hours

questions.explanation: Loss of compressibility is the key bedside sign of DVT. In a study of hospitalist-performed compression POCUS, sensitivity was 100% and specificity 95.8%, but in that low-prevalence cohort a positive scan had a positive predictive value of only about 62%. So do both: start anticoagulation now rather than waiting overnight for the vascular lab, and obtain the formal study to confirm—never forgo the formal study because of a bedside assessment.

why_not.B: Diagnostic POCUS should be confirmed by a formal study rather than used alone.
why_not.C: Waiting overnight delays treatment when her bedside findings already support DVT.
why_not.D: With a noncompressible vein already seen, a D-dimer would not change management.
why_not.E: Repeating the bedside scan delays treatment and still would not replace the formal study.

questions.pearl: Positive bedside DVT scan: start anticoagulation and still get the formal duplex—never forgo the formal study because of POCUS.

questions.topic: Nutrition risk screening in hospitalized older adults
questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted to the medical ward with severe community-acquired pneumonia. He requires 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula and intravenous antibiotics. Until this illness he was independent, ate three full meals a day, and had a stable weight for the past year. His body mass index is 34 kg/m². He has hypertension and osteoarthritis. On hospital day 1, the team reviews his nutrition plan.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate nutrition plan?

options.A: No intervention, because his body mass index is elevated
options.B: A calorie-restricted diet to promote weight loss
options.C: Nasogastric tube feeding to meet caloric goals
options.D: Defer intervention until he loses more than 5% of his weight

questions.explanation: The Nutrition Risk Score adds points for impaired nutritional status, severity of illness, and age, and 3 points is all it takes to be nutritionally at risk. A patient can earn no nutritional-status points and still be at risk if he has severe enough disease and is old enough—a high BMI, normal intake, and no weight loss do not exclude risk. In the EFFORT trial, dietitian-led, individualized support toward protein and calorie goals, begun within 48 hours of admission, reduced 30-day all-cause mortality from 10% to 7%.

why_not.A: A high BMI does not exclude nutritional risk; illness severity and age alone can put him at risk.
why_not.B: Acute illness raises nutritional needs; the goal is to meet protein and calorie targets, not to restrict them.
why_not.C: Oral, individualized support comes first; tube feeding is an escalation if targets are not met after about 5 days.
why_not.D: Waiting for weight loss misses risk that is already present from illness severity and age; screen and act within 48 hours.

questions.pearl: A high BMI doesn't exclude risk: severe illness plus age ≥70 can reach a Nutrition Risk Score of 3—start dietitian-led support early.

questions.topic: Preventing hospital-acquired debility
questions.stem:
An 82-year-old woman is admitted with acute pyelonephritis and is treated with intravenous ceftriaxone. Before admission she lived alone, walked independently with a cane, and was independent in all activities of daily living. She fell once last year without injury. On hospital day 2 she is alert and feels better. An admission order reads "bed rest" because of fall risk, and she has not been out of bed since arrival. Vital signs are shown.
Vital signValue
Temperature37.1 °C
Blood pressure128/72 mm Hg
Heart rate84/min
Oxygen saturation97% on room air
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate activity order?

options.A: Bed rest with a bed alarm to prevent falls
options.B: Bed rest until physical therapy evaluates her
options.C: Assisted hallway walks at least twice daily
options.D: Out of bed to a chair for meals
options.E: Bedside commode use, otherwise in bed

questions.explanation: Physicians can help prevent hospital-acquired debility—"movement is medicine." Nurses, patient care technicians, and physicians can help mobilize most patients, so a previously independent walker should not wait in bed for a therapist. In the VA STRIDE program of supervised walking, there was one fall in each group, and neither occurred during a walk. Ordering bed rest because "I don't know if they're safe to get out of bed" is a common reflex—and it is how patients get weaker in the hospital and are readmitted.

why_not.A: Bed rest promotes hospital-acquired debility, and in the STRIDE program no fall occurred during a supervised walk.
why_not.B: Nurses, patient care technicians, and physicians can mobilize most patients; waiting for therapy keeps a previously independent walker in bed.
why_not.D: Sitting up for meals is better than nothing but falls far short of the walking she needs to keep her function.
why_not.E: Confinement to the bed and commode is near-immobility and promotes the deconditioning that leads to readmission.

questions.pearl: Movement is medicine: don't default to bed rest for fall risk—get previously independent patients walking daily with staff help.

questions.topic: Titrating oral opioids for uncontrolled pain
questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is admitted with severe pain from a new lytic metastasis in the right iliac bone. She takes no opioids at home, and the state prescription drug monitoring program report shows no controlled-substance prescriptions. Kidney and liver function are normal. Scheduled acetaminophen has been started, and radiation oncology has been consulted. At 14:00 she receives oxycodone 5 mg orally. At 16:00 the nurse calls to report that the patient rates her pain 10/10, unchanged from before the dose. She is alert and conversant; respiratory rate is 18/min and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pain management?
questions.explanation: Oral opioids such as oxycodone peak at 60–90 minutes, so 2 hours after the dose its full effect has been seen—and it did nothing. The titration rule: increase the dose by 50% for moderate pain and 100% for severe pain. With no relief, double to oxycodone 10 mg and give it now rather than waiting for the next 4-hour slot. Tramadol, codeine, and meperidine carry more risk than benefit, and a fentanyl patch needs 12–24 hours to reach effective levels, so it cannot manage a pain crisis.

why_not.B: Waiting is unnecessary because the dose has already peaked, and repeating an ineffective dose does not escalate treatment.
why_not.C: Tramadol's risks outweigh its benefits because of unpredictable metabolism and side effects, with little added pain control.
why_not.D: A fentanyl patch needs 12–24 hours to reach effective levels and is contraindicated for acute pain and in opioid-naive patients.
why_not.E: Intramuscular opioids should be avoided; oral or intravenous routes are preferred.

questions.pearl: Oral opioids peak at 60–90 minutes: if a dose did nothing, double it and give it now—don't wait for the next scheduled interval.

questions.topic: Opioid rotation in acute kidney injury
questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with prostate cancer metastatic to the spine is hospitalized for a pain crisis. His pain has improved but is not fully controlled with morphine 4 mg intravenously every 3 hours as needed, which he uses about five times a day, along with scheduled acetaminophen. On hospital day 4, after a contrast-enhanced CT scan and several days of poor oral intake, his serum creatinine level rises from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.4 mg/dL. He is alert and oriented.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate as-needed opioid order now?

options.A: Continue morphine 4 mg IV every 3 hours as needed
options.B: Meperidine 50 mg IV every 3 hours as needed
options.C: Hydromorphone 4 mg IV every 3 hours as needed
options.D: Hydromorphone 0.6 mg IV every 3 hours as needed
options.E: Codeine 60 mg orally every 4 hours as needed

questions.explanation: Morphine should be avoided in kidney dysfunction because its metabolites build up and can be dangerous—even causing seizures. Rotate to another opioid using the equianalgesic table rather than swapping milligram for milligram: morphine 10 mg IV ≈ hydromorphone 1.5 mg IV, so 4 mg × 1.5 ÷ 10 = 0.6 mg IV. Hydromorphone 4 mg IV would be nearly seven times that dose. The result is an estimate: with his pain not fully controlled, the full converted dose is reasonable, whereas a more conservative prescriber may trim it to allow for cross-tolerance.

why_not.A: Morphine's metabolites accumulate when creatinine rises to 2.4 mg/dL; switch to a different opioid.
why_not.B: Meperidine's risks outweigh its benefits; its metabolite normeperidine accumulates in kidney injury and can cause seizures.
why_not.C: Swapping milligram for milligram ignores potency: 4 mg of IV hydromorphone is roughly 27 mg of IV morphine, an overdose risk.
why_not.E: Codeine's risks outweigh its benefits because of unpredictable metabolism, and its active metabolites accumulate in kidney dysfunction.

questions.pearl: Kidney injury on morphine? Rotate (e.g., to hydromorphone) with the equianalgesic table—4 mg IV morphine ≈ 0.6 mg IV hydromorphone, never mg-for-mg.

questions.topic: Preventing opioid-induced constipation
questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with pancreatic cancer and painful liver metastases is being discharged on oxycodone 5 mg orally every 4 hours as needed; in the hospital he has used four or five doses a day. He has a soft bowel movement daily and no abdominal pain or distention. Kidney function is normal. The team has provided naloxone and counseled him on safe storage.
questions.question: Which of the following bowel regimens is most appropriate to prescribe with the opioid?
questions.explanation: "The hand that writes the opioid writes the laxative." Nausea and fatigue from opioids usually fade within days, but constipation never gets better, so start a laxative with the opioid even when bowel habits are normal. Prevention starts with a stimulant laxative such as senna or bisacodyl; fiber and docusate should not be used for opioid-induced constipation.

why_not.A: Docusate doesn't work for opioid-induced constipation; in a randomized trial it added nothing to senna.
why_not.C: Fiber is not recommended for opioid-induced constipation.
why_not.D: Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are reserved for constipation that persists after senna and polyethylene glycol are maximized, not for prevention.
why_not.E: Opioid-induced constipation is easier to prevent than to treat, so prophylaxis should start with the first prescription.

questions.pearl: The hand that writes the opioid writes the laxative: start senna (± polyethylene glycol); docusate and fiber don't work for opioid-induced constipation.

questions.topic: Right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block
questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man with hypertension has a routine ECG before elective inguinal hernia repair. He has no chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or syncope and exercises without limitation. Blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg and heart rate 72/min. The ECG findings are summarized.
FeatureFinding
RhythmSinus, 72/min; PR interval 180 ms
QRS duration140 ms
Lead V1rsR′; the late (terminal) deflection is positive
Lead IPredominantly positive, with a broad, slurred terminal S wave
Lead V6Broad, slurred terminal S wave
Lead aVLqR
Leads II, III, and aVFrS, predominantly negative
Computed QRS axis−60°
ST segmentsNo ST elevation
questions.question: Which of the following best describes this ECG?

options.C: Right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block
options.D: Right bundle branch block with left posterior fascicular block

questions.explanation: Start with the wide QRS: its terminal (delayed) portion comes back toward V1 (rsR′), which identifies right bundle branch block; in left bundle branch block the delayed forces travel away from V1. Then the axis: lead I positive, aVF negative, and lead II negative places it beyond the normal range, so there is left axis deviation. Left anterior fascicular block shows up as left axis deviation, so a right bundle with left axis deviation (here −60°) indicates an accompanying left anterior fascicular block (right axis deviation would suggest left posterior fascicular block) and raises concern for more conduction-system disease.

why_not.A: An isolated right bundle branch block would not explain the marked left axis deviation (−60°).
why_not.B: In left bundle branch block the delayed terminal forces travel away from V1; here they return toward V1 (rsR′).
why_not.D: Right bundle branch block with left posterior fascicular block typically produces right axis deviation, not an axis of −60°.
why_not.E: An rsR′ with terminal forces directed toward V1 is a specific right bundle pattern, not a nonspecific delay.

questions.pearl: Right bundle branch block plus left axis deviation = add left anterior fascicular block; think more conduction-system disease.

questions.topic: Ventricular tachycardia vs SVT with aberrancy
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man with hypertension comes to the emergency department with 1 hour of palpitations. He is alert. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg, heart rate 160/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. His ECG from 1 year ago showed sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS complex. The current 12-lead ECG findings are summarized.
FeatureFinding
Rate and rhythmRegular, 160/min
QRSWide (160 ms), uniform morphology
P wavesSeen intermittently at a regular rate of 88/min, with no consistent relationship to the QRS complexes
One complexOccurs slightly early, is narrow and identical to his baseline sinus QRS, and is preceded by a P wave
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction and aberrancy
options.C: Sinus tachycardia with bundle branch block

questions.explanation: For a regular wide-complex tachycardia, the question is SVT with aberrancy versus VT. Here the P waves run at their own rate and do not conduct to the wide complexes, which is AV dissociation, one of the ways to identify VT with confidence. When a sinus impulse does get through, it conducts a narrow QRS: a capture beat, which is diagnostic of VT. Fusion beats are another clue that points to VT.

why_not.A: An idioventricular rhythm is not fast; a ventricular rhythm at 160/min is VT.
why_not.B: In 2:1 flutter, flutter waves conduct in a fixed ratio to every QRS; independent P waves with a capture beat indicate AV dissociation.
why_not.C: Sinus tachycardia would have a P wave before every QRS; here P waves at 88/min are unrelated to a ventricular rate of 160/min.
why_not.D: AV dissociation with a narrow capture beat points to a ventricular origin rather than SVT with aberrant conduction.

questions.pearl: Wide-complex tachycardia with AV dissociation or a narrow capture beat = VT.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 23: EKG Interpretation — Dr. Natalie Stokes, 8/4/2026 (slide 19; transcript excerpts 23_P014, 23_P013)

questions.topic: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
questions.stem:
A 74-year-old woman is admitted with 3 days of worsening dyspnea, cough, and purulent sputum. She has a 50-pack-year smoking history, and spirometry 1 year ago showed a postbronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.45 with an FEV1 of 35% of predicted. She is using accessory muscles and has diffuse expiratory wheezes. Respiratory rate is 28/min, blood pressure 142/80 mm Hg, heart rate 124/min and irregular, and oxygen saturation 86% on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. She is alert and has no chest pain. The ECG shows an irregularly irregular, narrow-complex rhythm at 124/min; a distinct P wave precedes every QRS complex, but the P waves vary in shape from beat to beat (at least three different morphologies), with varying PR intervals. Arterial blood gas results on 2 L/min of oxygen are shown.
TestResult
pH7.31
PaCO258 mm Hg
PaO252 mm Hg
Bicarbonate28 mEq/L
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: An irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with a P wave before every QRS, but with P waves that do not look the same because they are not all coming from the sinus node, is multifocal atrial tachycardia. Atrial activity is conducting to the ventricles, unlike AF, which is irregular without clear atrial activity. MAT should make you worry about hypoxia and think about the lungs: a COPD exacerbation, PE, or something similar. Treat that, rather than the heart rate itself.

why_not.A: Amiodarone targets the heart rate, but MAT is driven by her hypoxemia and lung disease, which are what need treatment.
why_not.C: Cardioversion is aimed at the rhythm and does nothing for the lung disease that is driving MAT.
why_not.D: This is not AF: a P wave precedes every QRS, so there is no AF indication for anticoagulation.
why_not.E: Adenosine acts on AV-nodal conduction, not on the hypoxemia and lung disease that are driving this rhythm.

questions.pearl: Irregular narrow tachycardia with a P before every QRS but changing P-wave shapes = MAT: treat the lungs, not the rate.

questions.topic: Low-risk acute chest pain
questions.stem: A 41-year-old man comes to the emergency department 5 hours after the onset of intermittent left-sided chest tightness that began at rest at his desk, with episodes lasting 10 to 15 minutes; he is now pain-free. He smokes cigarettes and has no other cardiovascular risk factors or known heart disease. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and heart rate 76/min; the physical examination is normal. The ECG is normal. High-sensitivity troponin I values at arrival and 2 hours later are both below the assay's 99th-percentile upper reference limit, with no meaningful change. A chest radiograph is normal. His HEART score is 2.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Admission for observation and stress testing

questions.explanation: Within a clinical decision pathway, a low HEART score (here 2) with initial and serial troponins below the assay's 99th percentile identifies a low-risk patient: the probability of an event in the next 30 days is low enough for early follow-up. The disposition is discharge with outpatient follow-up with cardiology or the PCP for further assessment of coronary disease. Patients who are not low risk need inpatient assessment with additional testing before discharge, and those at very high risk may need invasive evaluation.

why_not.A: Low-risk patients identified by a validated pathway do not need admission or urgent stress testing.
why_not.B: Urgent anatomic imaging is for intermediate-risk patients, not for someone already low risk by pathway and troponins.
why_not.D: Invasive assessment is for very high-risk patients, not for a patient who is low risk by pathway and troponins.
why_not.E: High-sensitivity troponins at arrival and 2 hours already complete the rule-out; waiting longer adds time without benefit.

questions.pearl: Low HEART score plus negative serial high-sensitivity troponins = low risk: discharge with prompt outpatient follow-up, no urgent testing.

questions.topic: Acute chest pain with a prior inconclusive stress test
questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes comes to the emergency department after 2 hours of substernal pressure at rest that has now resolved. She has no known heart disease. Vital signs and physical examination are normal. The ECG shows nonspecific T-wave flattening that is unchanged from a prior tracing. High-sensitivity troponin I values at arrival and at 2 hours are below the 99th-percentile upper reference limit without a significant change. Her HEART score is 5. Seven months ago, for exertional chest discomfort, she had an exercise SPECT myocardial perfusion study that was reported as inconclusive: she reached only 72% of her age-predicted maximal heart rate, and a small, mild inferior perfusion defect was thought to possibly represent diaphragmatic attenuation. No further testing was performed.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
questions.explanation: With acute chest pain, negative troponins, and a HEART score that is not low, she is at least intermediate risk, and the first question is whether there is prior cardiac testing. A prior test that was not clearly normal within the last year calls for repeat testing, and it is best to switch modality: after a stress test, choose an anatomic test, coronary CT angiography, so the result is less likely to fall into the same gray zone. A treadmill ECG alone has lower sensitivity and specificity than the other tests.

why_not.B: Her prior study was not clearly normal (submaximal and equivocal), so it cannot be used to justify discharge without testing.
why_not.C: A treadmill ECG has lower sensitivity and specificity than the other tests, and her last exercise study was already nondiagnostic.
why_not.D: Invasive angiography is for high-risk features or a clearly abnormal prior test, not an inconclusive study with negative troponins.
why_not.E: Repeating the same modality risks another gray-zone result; switching to anatomic testing is preferred.

questions.pearl: Intermediate-risk chest pain with an equivocal stress test in the past year: switch modality and obtain coronary CT angiography.

questions.topic: Suspected coronary microvascular disease (INOCA)
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman who smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily has had 8 months of exertional chest pressure that is relieved by rest. An exercise treadmill test reproduced her typical chest pressure, with 2-mm horizontal ST-segment depression in the lateral leads at a moderate workload. Coronary CT angiography showed smooth coronary arteries with only minimal nonobstructive plaque (<25% stenosis). Her symptoms persist, and her cardiologist wants to evaluate the cause of her ischemia.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?
questions.explanation: Ischemia on stress testing with no obstructive coronary disease raises the possibility of coronary microvascular disease, which is more frequent in women and in smokers. Assessing it requires objective quantification of myocardial blood flow, so stress PET, which quantifies flow, is the preferred noninvasive test, with cardiac MRI as an alternative. Her epicardial anatomy is already known to be nonobstructive, and the treadmill test has already shown ischemia, so repeating either adds nothing.

why_not.A: A calcium score measures calcified plaque, not microvascular blood flow.
why_not.C: Standard SPECT shows relative perfusion and does not provide the flow quantification needed to diagnose microvascular disease.
why_not.D: Her epicardial anatomy is already known to be nonobstructive; another anatomic study cannot assess the microvasculature.
why_not.E: The treadmill test has already shown ischemia; repeating it adds no information about the microvasculature.

questions.pearl: Ischemia without obstructive CAD: suspect microvascular disease and quantify myocardial blood flow; stress PET is the preferred noninvasive test.

questions.topic: Padua score and choice of VTE prophylaxis
questions.stem:
A 73-year-old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. She has been mostly confined to bed for 4 days at home and is expected to remain on bed rest for several more days. She has no history of cancer, venous thromboembolism, thrombophilia, recent surgery or trauma, myocardial infarction or stroke, or hormone therapy, and no history of bleeding. BMI is 27. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin12.2 g/dL
Platelet count245,000/µL
INR1.0
Estimated creatinine clearance52 mL/min
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis?

options.B: Unfractionated heparin 5000 units SC three times daily

questions.explanation: Her Padua score is 6: immobility = 3 points, acute infection = 1, heart failure = 1, and age ≥70 = 1. A score of ≥4 is high risk, so pharmacologic prophylaxis is indicated—missing the 3-point immobility item would wrongly label her low risk. With a creatinine clearance >30 and BMI <40, enoxaparin 40 mg once daily is the preferred prophylaxis: in a 2022 network meta-analysis, LMWH gave the best balance of benefit and harm, reducing symptomatic VTE without the excess bleeding seen with UFH or DOACs.

why_not.A: Counting 3 points for immobility gives a Padua score of 6 (high risk), so omitting prophylaxis would leave her unprotected.
why_not.B: UFH has a less favorable benefit–harm balance than LMWH and requires three injections a day.
why_not.D: Twice-daily 30-mg dosing is not needed for a medical patient with BMI <40 and adequate kidney function.
why_not.E: DOACs carry more bleeding risk and are not preferred over LMWH for inpatient prophylaxis.

questions.pearl: Count every Padua item—immobility alone scores 3; ≥4 is high risk. For medical patients, give enoxaparin 40 mg daily if BMI <40 and CrCl >30.

questions.topic: Refused VTE prophylaxis doses
questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is hospitalized with pneumonia and decompensated heart failure. He was bed-bound before admission, his Padua score is 5, and enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily was ordered on admission. On hospital day 3, the medication administration record shows that the second and third doses were documented as refused. He remains mostly in bed. When asked, he says, 'Nobody told me what that shot was for, and I already get stuck for labs every day.' Platelet count and kidney function are normal, and he has no bleeding.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Replace enoxaparin with sequential compression devices
options.B: Discuss the purpose of the injection and his concerns
options.C: Change to apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily
options.D: Document informed refusal and continue the current order
options.E: Change to aspirin 81 mg orally daily

questions.explanation: Missed doses are a common, modifiable quality gap: in one study 10% to 15% of ordered prophylaxis doses were never given, refusal is the largest contributor, and in a surgical cohort DVT risk rose as missed doses accumulated. Here the refusal stems from not knowing why the shot is given, so the next step is to talk with the patient—explain what the injection is for, understand his concerns, and work with him on an individualized plan. He is already on once-daily LMWH, so the drug itself does not need to change.

why_not.A: Mechanical devices are less effective than LMWH for a patient who can take it, and they are often not actually on.
why_not.C: DOACs are not preferred for inpatient prophylaxis in medical patients because of more bleeding.
why_not.D: His refusal is not yet informed—no one has explained the injection—and missed doses have been linked to more DVT.
why_not.E: Aspirin is not a guideline option for VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized medical patients.

questions.pearl: Check the MAR: refused prophylaxis doses are a modifiable gap—explain the purpose and address the patient's concerns.
references: MUH Noon Conference, Lecture 25: VTE Prevention — Dr. Ann Perrin, 8/6/2026 (slide 57; transcript excerpts 25_P013, 25_P015)
Louis SG et al. Missed Doses of Enoxaparin and Incidence of DVT, JAMA Surg 2014
Haut ER et al. Patient-Centered Education Bundle to Reduce Missed VTE Prophylaxis, JAMA Netw Open 2018

questions.topic: Extended VTE prophylaxis after a medical hospitalization
questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman is being discharged home after a 6-day hospitalization for pneumonia and acute decompensated heart failure, during which she received enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily. Her pneumonia has been fully treated, she is euvolemic on her home oxygen, and she is walking short distances with a walker. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, cancer, or thrombophilia, and she did not require ICU care. Her daughter asks whether she should continue a blood thinner at home because she read that clot risk persists for weeks after discharge. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin12.0 g/dL
Platelet count220,000/µL
Estimated creatinine clearance48 mL/min
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis plan at discharge?

options.B: Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily for 35 days
options.C: Rivaroxaban 10 mg orally daily for 35 days
options.D: Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily for 30 days
options.E: Aspirin 81 mg orally daily for 35 days

questions.explanation: The daughter is right that risk lingers—the increased VTE risk persists for 45 to 60 days after discharge in medical patients—but that does not justify routine extended prophylaxis. ASH recommends against routine extended-duration prophylaxis after a medical hospitalization. Rivaroxaban is FDA-approved for extended prophylaxis, but in the post-discharge MARINER trial it missed its primary endpoint, so it is not used routinely. For this improving, ambulating patient, the inpatient enoxaparin should simply be stopped at discharge.

why_not.B: Extended LMWH after a medical admission is not recommended routinely because added bleeding offsets the small reduction in VTE.
why_not.C: Although approved, extended rivaroxaban missed its primary endpoint in MARINER and is not recommended routinely.
why_not.D: DOACs are not recommended for extended prophylaxis after a medical hospitalization.
why_not.E: Aspirin is not a guideline-recommended VTE prophylaxis option for medical patients.

questions.pearl: After a medical hospitalization, stop prophylaxis at discharge—ASH recommends against routine extended-duration prophylaxis despite lingering post-discharge risk.

questions.topic: Anaphylaxis in a patient taking a beta-blocker
questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is hospitalized for cellulitis of the left leg. He has coronary artery disease with a myocardial infarction 3 years ago and takes metoprolol, aspirin, and atorvastatin. Ten minutes after his first dose of intravenous cefazolin begins, he develops generalized hives, lip swelling, wheezing, and lightheadedness, and the infusion is stopped. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg (128/74 mm Hg earlier today), pulse is 94/min, respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on ambient air. He has diffuse expiratory wheezes and widespread urticaria. The nurse asks whether epinephrine is safe given his heart disease and beta-blocker.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh
options.D: Subcutaneous epinephrine into the upper arm

questions.explanation: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, and there are no absolute contraindications—coronary disease and beta-blocker use are not reasons to withhold or delay it. The adult dose is 0.3–0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL epinephrine given intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (outer thigh), not subcutaneously. H1 antihistamines such as diphenhydramine can relieve cutaneous symptoms but lack randomized trial support in anaphylaxis. Glucagon is reserved for beta-blocked patients who are not responding to epinephrine; it is not a substitute for the first dose.

why_not.A: Antihistamines relieve hives and itching but do not reverse hypotension or bronchospasm, so they are only adjuncts after epinephrine.
why_not.C: Glucagon is for beta-blocked patients whose anaphylaxis fails to respond to epinephrine, not a replacement for the first dose.
why_not.D: Epinephrine should be injected intramuscularly into the thigh; subcutaneous injection reaches peak levels much more slowly.
why_not.E: Glucocorticoids are slow-acting adjuncts and should never be given in place of epinephrine for acute anaphylaxis.

questions.pearl: Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg into the lateral thigh first—no absolute contraindications, even with coronary disease or a beta-blocker.

questions.topic: Observation after severe anaphylaxis
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after a yellow jacket sting on his forearm. He has generalized hives, lip swelling, and diffuse wheezing; blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg and pulse is 124/min. He receives intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous normal saline, and a second dose of intramuscular epinephrine 10 minutes later for persistent hypotension. His symptoms then resolve completely. One hour after resolution, blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, the lungs are clear, and the hives have faded. He feels well and asks to go home. Epinephrine autoinjectors have been prescribed.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge now; 1 symptom-free hour is enough
options.B: Give oral prednisone and discharge now
options.C: Give a third dose of intramuscular epinephrine
options.E: Give oral cetirizine and discharge now

questions.explanation: Biphasic anaphylaxis is a recurrence of symptoms after apparent complete resolution, without further exposure. A more severe initial reaction and needing more than one dose of epinephrine are its key risk factors, and he had both (hypotension, two doses). When risk factors are present, observation for about 6 hours is recommended rather than discharge after 1 hour. There are no data to support antihistamines or glucocorticoids for preventing biphasic anaphylaxis, so prescribing them does not make early discharge safe.

why_not.A: His severe reaction and need for two epinephrine doses raise the risk of a biphasic reaction, so 1 hour of observation is too short.
why_not.B: No data support glucocorticoids for preventing biphasic anaphylaxis, so they do not replace extended observation.
why_not.C: He is now asymptomatic; epinephrine treats active anaphylaxis and is not given pre-emptively to prevent recurrence.
why_not.E: No data support antihistamines for preventing biphasic anaphylaxis, so they do not replace extended observation.

questions.pearl: Severe anaphylaxis or >1 epinephrine dose: observe about 6 hours; antihistamines and steroids are not proven to prevent biphasic reactions.

questions.topic: Angioedema in a long-term ACE inhibitor user
questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with swelling of her lips and tongue that she noticed on waking and that has slowly worsened over the past 14 hours. She has no itching, rash, wheezing, or abdominal pain. She ate shrimp for dinner the night before, as she does most weeks. Her only medication is lisinopril, which she has taken for hypertension for 6 years. Paramedics gave intramuscular epinephrine, intravenous diphenhydramine, and intravenous methylprednisolone without improvement. Vital signs are normal, and oxygen saturation is 98% on ambient air. She speaks in full sentences without stridor, and there is no urticaria. Flexible laryngoscopy shows no laryngeal edema. Over the next day the swelling gradually resolves.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her antihypertensive therapy?

options.C: Continue lisinopril and add daily cetirizine
options.D: Continue lisinopril; carry an epinephrine autoinjector
options.E: Stop lisinopril; avoid all ACE inhibitors

questions.explanation: Angioedema without hives or itching that worsens insidiously over many hours points to a bradykinin-mediated process, which typically does not respond to epinephrine, antihistamines, or steroids—exactly what happened here. Allergic (mast cell–mediated) angioedema, as from a food, typically comes with hives and peaks within 1–2 hours. ACE inhibitor angioedema can occur at any time during therapy, even after years, so long tolerance does not exonerate lisinopril. She must stop it and strictly avoid the entire ACE inhibitor class.

why_not.A: Mast cell–mediated reactions to shellfish typically bring hives and peak within 1–2 hours, and she eats shrimp most weeks; this slow, hive-free swelling points to lisinopril.
why_not.B: ACE inhibitor angioedema is a class effect, so switching to another ACE inhibitor exposes her to the same risk.
why_not.C: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema does not respond to antihistamines, and continuing lisinopril leaves the cause in place.
why_not.D: Epinephrine does not reliably treat bradykinin-mediated angioedema, so an autoinjector would not protect her while she stays on lisinopril.

questions.pearl: Hive-free, slowly worsening angioedema on an ACE inhibitor—even after years—is likely bradykinin-mediated: stop it and avoid the whole class.
