questions.topic: Chronic spontaneous urticaria
questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had itchy hives on most days for the past 3 months. Individual wheals fade within 24 hours and leave no bruising, and she has had no blistering, fever, joint pain, or lip or tongue swelling. She cannot identify a trigger and wonders whether a new food allergy is responsible. Cetirizine 10 mg taken as needed gives partial, short-lived relief. She takes no other medications. Examination shows several raised, blanching, erythematous wheals with central swelling on the trunk and arms; the rest of the examination is normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.C: Daily cetirizine, increased up to fourfold
options.E: Punch biopsy of a representative wheal

questions.explanation: Hives occurring continuously or intermittently for more than 6 weeks define chronic urticaria, which is often idiopathic; IgE-mediated food allergy is a cause of acute urticaria, so a food-specific IgE panel is not the next step. Treatment is a step-up approach: a daily non-sedating H1 antihistamine (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, or loratadine), increased up to four times the standard dose, with omalizumab added if high-dose antihistamines fail.

why_not.A: Chronic urticaria is often idiopathic; IgE-mediated food allergy causes acute episodes, not months of near-daily hives.
why_not.B: Systemic steroids are not the step-up treatment for chronic urticaria; daily, up-dosed H1 antihistamines come first.
why_not.D: Omalizumab is the next step only after daily high-dose H1 antihistamines fail.
why_not.E: Short-lived blanching wheals without fever, bruising, blistering, or severe joint pain do not suggest another process requiring biopsy.

questions.pearl: Hives >6 weeks are often idiopathic: daily non-sedating H1 antihistamine up to 4× dose, then omalizumab—skip the food-allergy panel.

questions.topic: Alcoholic hallucinosis vs delirium tremens
questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with cellulitis of the left leg. He had been drinking about a pint of vodka daily until his last drink 24 hours ago. He now reports seeing and feeling insects crawling on his arms and bedsheets and is distressed by them. He is alert, oriented to person, place, and date, recites the months of the year backward without error, and follows the conversation normally. He is diaphoretic and has a fine bilateral hand tremor. There is no nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, or ataxia. Serum glucose and electrolyte levels are normal. Vital signs are shown.
Vital signValue
Temperature37.4 °C
Heart rate104/min
Blood pressure148/92 mm Hg
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis can develop within the first day of withdrawal and usually consists of tactile or visual hallucinations—often things crawling on the skin—independent of delirium: patients remain able to answer questions and stay oriented. Delirium is mandatory to diagnose delirium tremens, which typically develops about 48 hours after the last drink. Clinicians sometimes diagnose delirium tremens just because withdrawal is severe, but the label has implications for future placement.

why_not.A: Delirium is required for delirium tremens; his attention and orientation are intact, and DTs typically appear about 48 hours after the last drink.
why_not.B: Hallucinations beginning within a day of stopping heavy drinking, with tremor and autonomic signs, point to alcohol withdrawal rather than a primary psychiatric illness.
why_not.D: Wernicke encephalopathy causes an altered mental status, and he is fully alert and attentive without eye-movement abnormalities or ataxia.
why_not.E: Uncomplicated withdrawal is tremulousness with autonomic signs; new hallucinations with a clear sensorium define a distinct manifestation, hallucinosis.

questions.pearl: Hallucinations with a clear sensorium = alcoholic hallucinosis. No delirium, no delirium tremens.

questions.topic: Benzodiazepine-resistant alcohol withdrawal
questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and prior withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens requiring intensive care presents to the emergency department 30 hours after his last drink. He is tremulous, diaphoretic, and severely agitated, pulling at his intravenous line. Thiamine has been given, and point-of-care glucose is 112 mg/dL. Over the past hour he received diazepam 20 mg IV, then 40 mg IV, then 80 mg IV, about 15 minutes apart, with minimal improvement in agitation or vital signs. He is protecting his airway. Current vital signs are shown.
Vital signValue
Temperature37.7 °C
Heart rate128/min
Blood pressure176/104 mm Hg
Respiratory rate20/min
Oxygen saturation97% on room air
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: For a patient who presents already in withdrawal, IV diazepam can be front-loaded and titrated to response—doubling the dose every 10–15 minutes when there is little response, up to about 80–100 mg per dose—with close monitoring. When a patient needs that much and is not responding, benzodiazepines are probably no longer the best choice—escalate to phenobarbital, which directly activates GABA-A receptors. A strategy of escalating benzodiazepines plus phenobarbital was associated with less need for mechanical ventilation in delirium tremens.

why_not.A: A fixed schedule is a "set it and forget it" approach that under-treats escalating withdrawal and does not overcome benzodiazepine resistance.
why_not.B: Symptom-triggered oral dosing suits mild or absent symptoms; scales such as CIWA-Ar are less useful in severely ill, agitated patients.
why_not.C: He is protecting his airway; phenobarbital, given with close monitoring, aims to control withdrawal without mechanical ventilation.
why_not.D: Guidelines advise against oral or intravenous alcohol for preventing or treating alcohol withdrawal.

questions.pearl: No response after diazepam doubled to about 80–100 mg per dose signals benzodiazepine resistance—escalate to phenobarbital, with close monitoring.

questions.topic: Buprenorphine-precipitated opioid withdrawal
questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man with opioid use disorder who smokes and injects fentanyl daily is hospitalized for a forearm abscess and asks to start buprenorphine. Ten hours after his last fentanyl use, he has mild withdrawal (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale [COWS] score 7) and is given buprenorphine-naloxone 8 mg/2 mg sublingually. Twenty minutes later he is vomiting and has diarrhea, diffuse myalgias, rhinorrhea, yawning, piloerection, and dilated pupils; he is restless and tearful. He says, "It must be the naloxone in that pill." Current findings are shown.
FindingValue
COWS score26
Heart rate112/min
Blood pressure146/90 mm Hg
Respiratory rate18/min
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Intravenous naloxone to reverse the buprenorphine
options.C: Oral naltrexone to block opioid receptors
options.D: Methadone 80 mg orally as a single dose
options.E: Withhold opioid agonists for the next 72 hours

questions.explanation: Given while fentanyl is still active and withdrawal is only mild, buprenorphine is "going to knock all that off" the receptors, producing precipitated withdrawal. The naloxone in buprenorphine-naloxone is not the cause: it is there to deter dissolving and injecting the tablet, and under the tongue too little is absorbed to have a clinical effect. Management is counterintuitive—give more buprenorphine, plus ancillary medications for symptoms, including benzodiazepines or antipsychotics as needed. Once through it, he can continue buprenorphine if he is willing.

why_not.B: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist and would deepen the withdrawal; there is no opioid toxicity to reverse.
why_not.C: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist and would worsen withdrawal in an opioid-dependent patient.
why_not.D: Methadone accumulates over several days, so it is started low and increased gradually; 80 mg as a first dose risks overdose.
why_not.E: Leaving severe withdrawal untreated is unnecessary and risks losing him from care; more buprenorphine plus ancillary drugs relieves it.

questions.pearl: Precipitated withdrawal comes from buprenorphine displacing fentanyl, not from the naloxone—treat it with more buprenorphine plus ancillary medications.

questions.topic: Starting methadone during hospitalization
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with opioid use disorder who injects fentanyl is admitted with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus tricuspid-valve endocarditis and will need 4 to 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotics. She is in moderate opioid withdrawal. Two years ago she did well on methadone at an opioid treatment program, and she asks to restart it; she declines buprenorphine because of a previous episode of precipitated withdrawal. She has a government-issued identification card and lives on a bus line near her former program. Her baseline QTc interval is 430 ms.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for her opioid use disorder?

options.A: Methadone for up to 72 hours, then switch to clonidine
options.B: Start methadone now; arrange program intake before discharge
options.C: Defer methadone until outpatient program enrollment
options.D: Start methadone and prescribe a 30-day supply at discharge
options.E: Clonidine alone, because methadone requires program enrollment

questions.explanation: When a patient is hospitalized for another condition—here, endocarditis—clinicians can start methadone or buprenorphine and continue it for as long as she is in the hospital. Opioid agonist treatment is associated with about a 50% reduction in mortality, and starting it in the hospital is associated with fewer departures against medical advice and more completed treatment for the condition that brought the patient in. Because hospital clinicians cannot prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder at discharge, start it when she can reach a program afterward, as here, and arrange intake before she leaves.

why_not.A: No 72-hour limit applies to a patient hospitalized for another condition; methadone can continue for the whole stay.
why_not.C: Deferring leaves withdrawal untreated and forgoes a medication associated with a 50% mortality reduction and better completion of endocarditis treatment.
why_not.D: Hospital clinicians cannot prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder at discharge; continued dosing must come from an opioid treatment program.
why_not.E: Methadone can legally be started in the hospital; withdrawal care should be the beginning of opioid use disorder treatment, not a stand-alone event.

questions.pearl: Admitted for another illness? Start methadone or buprenorphine in the hospital, continue it all stay, and hand off to a treatment program before discharge.

questions.topic: Morning prednisone–induced hyperglycemia: matching insulin to the steroid
questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is hospitalized with an exacerbation of COPD and is receiving prednisone 40 mg each morning. His home metformin is being held; hemoglobin A1c is 7.2%. He is eating full meals. His only insulin is correction-scale insulin lispro before meals. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Point-of-care glucose values over the past 2 days are shown.
TimeGlucose
Fasting (7 AM)112–124 mg/dL
Before lunch208–226 mg/dL
Before dinner286–312 mg/dL
Bedtime164–182 mg/dL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his insulin regimen?

options.C: Change to a high-dose correction scale

questions.explanation: With a morning dose of prednisone, fasting glucose is normal, values rise progressively from meal to meal, and they settle by bedtime—exactly this patient's pattern. Match the insulin to the steroid: give NPH at the same time as the prednisone dose so its action tracks the steroid's effect. Long-acting basal insulin such as glargine is better suited to dexamethasone or to longer-acting or twice-daily steroids. Relying on correction-scale insulin alone is reactive rather than proactive.

why_not.B: Glargine suits dexamethasone or longer-acting or twice-daily steroids; it can be dosed only to a normal fasting glucose, which he already has.
why_not.C: Correction-scale insulin alone is reactive rather than proactive and is discouraged.
why_not.D: Bedtime correction is avoided with morning steroids, whose effect wanes overnight.
why_not.E: Premixed insulin is avoided in the hospital because its short-acting component causes hypoglycemia when meals are missed.

questions.pearl: Morning prednisone causes normal fasting and afternoon–evening hyperglycemia: give NPH at the same time as the steroid dose.

questions.topic: Home premixed insulin in a hospitalized patient
questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is hospitalized with a diabetic foot infection. At home she takes premixed insulin 70/30 (NPH/regular), 24 units before breakfast and 16 units before dinner; hemoglobin A1c is 8.6%. She is eating, but she is expected to be made NPO intermittently over the next several days for imaging and possible surgical debridement. Since admission she has received only correction-scale insulin lispro, and her glucose values have ranged from 238 to 312 mg/dL. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate inpatient insulin regimen?

options.C: Glargine equal to her total home dose

questions.explanation: Premixed insulin is avoided in the hospital: its short-acting component (the 30 in 70/30) causes hypoglycemia when the patient is made NPO or sent for procedures. Patients admitted on premixed insulin are changed to basal-bolus insulin—basal plus mealtime and correction insulin, with roughly a 50:50 basal-to-bolus ratio—and can go back on the premix at discharge. Her persistent hyperglycemia also illustrates why correction-scale insulin alone is discouraged.

why_not.A: The short-acting component of 70/30 causes hypoglycemia when she is made NPO or sent for procedures.
why_not.B: Correction-scale insulin alone is discouraged and has already failed to control her glucose.
why_not.C: Giving her whole daily dose as basal insulin is basal-heavy; aim for roughly a 50:50 basal-to-bolus split.
why_not.D: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia, and oral agents are generally not appropriate in the hospital.

questions.pearl: Convert home premixed insulin to basal-bolus insulin in the hospital; avoid premix and sliding scale alone.

questions.topic: Overnight hypoglycemia on basal-bolus insulin in type 1 diabetes
questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is hospitalized with pyelonephritis and is improving with intravenous antibiotics. She is eating full meals. Her insulin regimen is insulin glargine 24 units at 9 PM and insulin lispro 6 units with each meal plus correction-scale lispro before meals; no bedtime correction doses have been given. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Yesterday's fasting glucose was 76 mg/dL. At 3 AM today her glucose was 58 mg/dL and was treated with juice; this morning's fasting glucose is 104 mg/dL. Her premeal and bedtime values have been 120 to 170 mg/dL.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her insulin regimen?

options.E: Stop prandial lispro; keep glargine unchanged

questions.explanation: Overnight and fasting lows point to the basal insulin—fasting glucose is what guides glargine adjustment. With two values below 80 mg/dL, lower the dose by about 20% and reassess rather than holding it. Completely holding insulin after hypoglycemia leads to high glucose at the following meals and the next day, and in type 1 diabetes, withholding insulin risks diabetic ketoacidosis. Her daytime values are at goal, so the prandial doses are not the problem.

why_not.A: Holding basal insulin in type 1 diabetes leads to high glucose the next day and risks diabetic ketoacidosis.
why_not.B: Two values below 80 mg/dL, including a 3 AM low, require a dose reduction.
why_not.D: Correction insulin alone removes the basal insulin that every patient with type 1 diabetes needs.
why_not.E: Her daytime values are at goal and she eats full meals; the overnight lows point to the basal dose.

questions.pearl: After hypoglycemia, adjust—don't hold—insulin; fasting values guide basal insulin, and type 1 diabetes always needs basal insulin.

questions.topic: Escalating from correction insulin in a hospitalized patient without diabetes
questions.stem: A 74-year-old man without a history of diabetes mellitus is hospitalized on the medical ward with community-acquired pneumonia. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.2%. He is eating most of his meals and is not receiving glucocorticoids. Because his admission glucose was 186 mg/dL, correction-scale insulin lispro before meals was ordered. Over the past 24 hours, his point-of-care glucose values were 214, 238, 196, and 228 mg/dL. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in glycemic management?

options.B: Change to a high-dose correction scale
options.D: Add scheduled basal and prandial insulin

questions.explanation: For a hospitalized patient without a prior history of diabetes, starting with correction insulin when glucose exceeds 140 mg/dL is reasonable. But once there are two or more values ≥180 mg/dL within 24 hours, add scheduled insulin, and avoid therapeutic inertia—hyperglycemia snowballs and becomes harder to control. Because oral agent therapy is generally not appropriate in the inpatient setting, the next step is scheduled basal and prandial insulin rather than metformin or a sulfonylurea.

why_not.A: Two or more values of 180 mg/dL or higher in 24 hours call for scheduled insulin, not more of the same.
why_not.B: A larger correction scale is still correction insulin alone; scheduled insulin is needed.
why_not.C: Oral agents are generally not appropriate in the hospital, and metformin can accumulate if creatinine rises.
why_not.E: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia, and oral agents are generally avoided in the hospital.

questions.pearl: Without known diabetes, correction insulin is a reasonable start—but two or more glucose values ≥180 mg/dL in 24 hours means add scheduled insulin.

questions.topic: Oxygen and carbon dioxide targets after ROSC
questions.stem:
A 61-year-old woman has return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after 8 minutes of CPR for an in-hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest. She is intubated and receiving volume-control ventilation with a tidal volume of 450 mL, respiratory rate 14/min, PEEP 5 cm H2O, and FiO2 1.0. Chest radiography shows the endotracheal tube 4 cm above the carina and no pneumothorax. A radial arterial line shows a mean arterial pressure of 70 mm Hg on norepinephrine 0.05 mcg/kg/min, and the pulse oximeter has a good waveform and reads 100%. An arterial blood gas obtained 30 minutes after ROSC is shown.
TestResult
pH7.20
PaCO250 mm Hg
PaO2312 mm Hg
Bicarbonate19 mEq/L
Lactate4.8 mmol/L
questions.question: Which of the following ventilator adjustments is most appropriate?

options.A: Decrease FiO2 and increase the respiratory rate
options.B: Decrease FiO2 and decrease the respiratory rate
options.C: Decrease FiO2 and keep the respiratory rate unchanged
options.D: Keep FiO2 at 1.0 and increase the respiratory rate
options.E: Keep FiO2 at 1.0 and decrease the respiratory rate

questions.explanation: After ROSC, oxygenate while avoiding hyperoxia, which can add to reperfusion injury; start high and titrate down once oxygenation can be measured reliably (here, an arterial line and a good pulse-oximeter signal). Targets are SpO2 90–98% or PaO2 60–105 mm Hg, so a PaO2 of 312 calls for lowering FiO2. The ventilation goal is a normal PaCO2 of 35–45 mm Hg; her PaCO2 of 50 adds respiratory acidosis to lactic acidosis, and severe acidosis blunts vasopressor effect, so minute ventilation should increase. Both changes are needed.

why_not.B: Lowering the rate would raise PaCO2 further and worsen her acidemia.
why_not.C: Corrects the hyperoxemia but leaves PaCO2 above the 35–45 mm Hg target despite acidemia.
why_not.D: Corrects ventilation but leaves her hyperoxemic even though oxygenation is now reliably measured.
why_not.E: Maintains hyperoxemia and worsens hypercapnia and acidemia.

questions.pearl: After ROSC: titrate FiO2 to SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105) once measurable, and ventilate to PaCO2 35–45 — avoid hyperoxia and hypercapnia.

questions.topic: Temperature control in patients who remain comatose after ROSC
questions.stem: A 54-year-old man has a witnessed out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest. Bystander CPR begins immediately, and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) occurs after 2 shocks (about 14 minutes). In the emergency department, he is intubated using rocuronium and started on a propofol infusion. Three hours after ROSC, he is in the ICU; train-of-four testing shows 4 of 4 twitches, and the propofol infusion has been off for 30 minutes. He does not open his eyes or follow commands but withdraws to pain; pupillary and corneal reflexes are present. Temperature is 37.8°C, mean arterial pressure is 72 mm Hg on norepinephrine 0.04 mcg/kg/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on FiO2 0.4. ECG shows no ST-segment elevation, and head CT shows no acute abnormality. A team member suggests no temperature management, noting that the TTM2 trial found hypothermia did not improve survival.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate temperature management?

options.B: Active cooling to a target of 30°C
options.D: Prophylactic levetiracetam in place of temperature control
options.E: No temperature intervention until EEG results return

questions.explanation: He is not following commands after sedation and paralysis have worn off, so he needs deliberate temperature control. The AHA range is 32°C to 37.5°C, with a class 2a recommendation to maintain it for at least 36 hours. TTM found no mortality difference between 33°C and 36°C, and TTM2 found no difference between hypothermia and normothermia, but the normothermia arm still actively treated fever. Temperature management is "targeted, not cool everyone": the goal is fever prevention with an individualized target, not abandoning temperature control.

why_not.A: Waiting until 39°C permits fever; even TTM2's normothermia arm actively treated fever.
why_not.B: 30°C is below the 32°C to 37.5°C range; cooling is not benign and can worsen hemodynamic instability and coagulopathy.
why_not.D: Anticonvulsants do not substitute for temperature control; seizures are detected with EEG monitoring and treated when present.
why_not.E: The decision rests on his bedside neurologic exam; temperature control should not wait for EEG results.

questions.pearl: Comatose after ROSC: deliberate temperature control at 32–37.5°C with fever prevention — 'targeted, not cool everyone,' but never 'no temperature management.'

questions.topic: Timing of neuroprognostication and sedation confounding after cardiac arrest
questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman remains comatose after an out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after about 20 minutes. She was cooled to 33°C for 36 hours and then rewarmed. Because propofol caused hypotension, she received continuous midazolam and fentanyl infusions for 60 hours; both were stopped 14 hours ago. Her course has been complicated by acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.4 mg/dL) and ischemic hepatitis (ALT 1240 U/L). It is now 76 hours after ROSC. She does not open her eyes or move to pain; pupillary and corneal reflexes are present. Continuous EEG shows a continuous background without seizures or burst suppression, and head CT on day 1 showed preserved gray–white differentiation. Her family asks whether she will wake up, noting that 72 hours have now passed.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the family?

options.A: More than 72 hours have passed without a motor response, so recovery is unlikely
options.B: A neuron-specific enolase level sent today will be the deciding test
options.C: A brain MRI obtained today will be the deciding test
options.D: Sedatives may still be masking her exam, so it is too early to judge
options.E: Her normal head CT on day 1 means she will probably wake up

questions.explanation: Never prognosticate too early. Outcome prediction should be delayed, generally at least 72 hours after ROSC or return to normothermia, and should be multimodal (examination, EEG, imaging, and other testing); no single biomarker, MRI, or early CT settles the question. The clock is not the only requirement: sedation and metabolic abnormalities confound the exam, and a benzodiazepine infusion can take days to clear and cloud neuroprognostication. Fourteen hours after a 60-hour midazolam infusion, with kidney and liver injury, her motor exam is not yet interpretable. Convey how ill she is, but avoid definitive statements.

why_not.A: Seventy-two hours is a minimum, not a trigger; residual midazolam with kidney and liver injury still confounds her motor exam.
why_not.B: No single biomarker should decide prognosis; neuroprognostication must be multimodal.
why_not.C: No single test, including MRI, decides prognosis; imaging must be integrated with other data.
why_not.E: A normal early CT does not exclude hypoxic-ischemic injury, and no single test predicts recovery; avoid definitive statements either way.

questions.pearl: Prognosticate no earlier than 72 hours after ROSC or normothermia, multimodally, and only after sedation and metabolic confounders clear — benzodiazepine infusions linger.

questions.topic: MSSA bacteremia with a penicillin allergy label
questions.stem: A 71-year-old man in the intensive care unit 6 days after coronary artery bypass grafting develops a temperature of 39.0 °C, blood pressure of 90/50 mm Hg, and heart rate of 120/min. A femoral central venous catheter placed 5 days ago is being removed. Two of 2 peripheral blood culture sets grow gram-positive cocci in clusters, and intravenous vancomycin is started. A rapid molecular blood culture panel identifies Staphylococcus aureus; mecA and mecC are not detected. His allergy list states “penicillin—itchy rash as a child.” He has no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or blistering or mucosal skin reactions.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic management?
questions.explanation: S. aureus without mecA is MSSA, and cefazolin is first-line therapy. Vancomycin has some MSSA activity but is not first line for MSSA bloodstream infection. A penicillin label should not keep him on vancomycin: cefazolin doesn’t share a side chain with any other beta-lactam, and for a lower-risk history such as a remote childhood rash, a non-cross-reacting drug can be given (or a graded challenge performed) without desensitization.

why_not.A: Vancomycin is inferior to a beta-lactam for MSSA bacteremia and should be changed once MSSA is identified.
why_not.B: Daptomycin is an alternative for patients who cannot receive a beta-lactam, which is not the case here.
why_not.D: Linezolid is not a first-line agent for S. aureus bacteremia.
why_not.E: Desensitization is unnecessary because cefazolin can be given directly despite a remote, low-risk penicillin rash.

questions.pearl: MSSA bacteremia: switch to cefazolin, even with a low-risk penicillin label—cefazolin shares no side chain with other beta-lactams.

questions.topic: Pseudomonas coverage in pneumonia
questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD and coronary artery disease is admitted with several days of fever, productive cough, and dyspnea. Temperature is 38.6 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula; he does not use oxygen at baseline. Expiration is prolonged, and breath sounds are decreased on the left. Chest radiograph shows a left lower lobe infiltrate. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are started. Records from another health system then arrive: he was hospitalized for pneumonia 6 weeks ago and treated with 7 days of ceftriaxone, and 3 days ago he was seen in an emergency department and discharged on oral cefpodoxime. A sputum culture from that visit is growing many Pseudomonas aeruginosa; susceptibilities are pending. He has no drug allergies.
questions.question: Which of the following should replace ceftriaxone?
questions.explanation: His recent sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, so his regimen needs an antipseudomonal agent. Ceftriaxone has good streptococcal and gram-negative activity, which is why it is used for community-acquired pneumonia, but it lacks pseudomonal activity. Cefepime has both pseudomonal and gram-positive activity, making it the best replacement here. Ertapenem covers ESBL-producing organisms but not Pseudomonas or Enterococcus.

why_not.B: Ampicillin-sulbactam has no activity against Pseudomonas.
why_not.C: Ceftaroline adds MRSA activity but does not cover Pseudomonas.
why_not.D: Ertapenem covers ESBL-producing organisms but not Pseudomonas.
why_not.E: Aminoglycosides are not primary therapy; at most they are a second agent, such as in septic shock while cultures are pending.

questions.pearl: Ceftriaxone and ertapenem miss Pseudomonas; when prior cultures grow it, switch to an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime.

questions.topic: Duration of therapy for gram-negative bacteremia
questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is hospitalized with pyelonephritis. Two of 2 blood culture sets and a urine culture grow Escherichia coli susceptible to ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Renal ultrasonography shows no hydronephrosis or abscess. After 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone, she has been afebrile for 36 hours, has normal vital signs, and is eating well. She is not immunocompromised and has no indwelling devices. The team plans to switch her to oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for discharge.
questions.question: What total duration of antibiotic therapy, counted from the first day of effective therapy, is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The BALANCE trial, the largest trial of bacteremia duration, compared 7 versus 14 days for non-staphylococcal bloodstream infections and found no difference. With source control and clinical improvement, 7 days total is sufficient for many bloodstream infections. Once she is stable, she can switch to a highly bioavailable oral agent such as TMP-SMX, and the intravenous days count toward the total—you don't restart the clock when changing to oral therapy.

why_not.A: Three days is too short for bacteremia; the evidence supports 7 days.
why_not.C: Ten days adds antibiotic exposure without benefit over 7 days in an improving patient.
why_not.D: BALANCE found 14 days no better than 7 days for non-staphylococcal bacteremia.
why_not.E: Prolonged courses are reserved for complicated foci such as abscess or endovascular infection, which she lacks.

questions.pearl: Gram-negative bacteremia with source control and improvement: 7 days total; IV days count after the oral switch.

questions.topic: Vaso-occlusive crisis in hemoglobin SC disease
questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with hemoglobin SC disease comes to the emergency department with severe pain in her lower back and both thighs that woke her at 3 AM. She rates it 9/10, says it feels like her usual pain crises, and took her home oxycodone without relief. Her chart contains an individualized care plan from her hematologist specifying an intravenous hydromorphone dose with repeat doses every 30 minutes as needed. Temperature is 37.2 °C, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, pulse is 108/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on ambient air. The lungs are clear, and there is no joint swelling or focal bone tenderness. Hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL (her baseline is 11–12 g/dL), leukocyte count is 10,900/µL, and platelet count is 410,000/µL. The emergency physician notes that her hemoglobin is near normal and questions whether she is truly in crisis.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Give hydromorphone per her care plan now
options.B: Withhold opioids because her hemoglobin is normal
options.C: Send haptoglobin to confirm active hemolysis
options.D: Give low-dose morphine; reassess in 4 hours
options.E: Discharge with ibuprofen and clinic follow-up

questions.explanation: No laboratory test objectively confirms a vaso-occlusive crisis, so the diagnosis rests on the patient's report. Genotype matters: a patient with HbSC can have a hemoglobin of about 12 g/dL and still be in crisis—'your hemoglobin is fine' does not exclude one. Acute management centers on rapid initiation of opioid therapy, with the regimen selected from her prior opioid-response history, which her individualized care plan captures. Delaying opioids while seeking laboratory 'proof' is the error to avoid.

why_not.B: No laboratory value confirms or excludes a crisis, and people with HbSC run higher hemoglobin levels than those with HbSS.
why_not.C: Haptoglobin is typically low in sickle cell disease even when patients are well, so it cannot confirm a crisis.
why_not.D: An arbitrary low dose with infrequent reassessment undertreats severe pain; her known effective regimen with frequent re-dosing should be used.
why_not.E: Severe pain unrelieved by home oxycodone needs prompt parenteral opioids, not discharge on an NSAID.

questions.pearl: No lab confirms a pain crisis—know the genotype, believe the patient, and start the care-plan opioid regimen rapidly.

questions.topic: Acute anemia in sickle cell anemia
questions.stem:
A 22-year-old man with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) comes to the emergency department with 4 days of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and lightheadedness. One week ago he had fever, headache, and myalgias that resolved on their own. He has mild low-back pain similar to his usual pain. He takes folic acid, does not take hydroxyurea, and has not been transfused in over a year. Temperature is 37.0 °C, blood pressure is 112/64 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate is 20/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on ambient air. He has conjunctival pallor; the lungs are clear, and neither the liver nor the spleen is palpable. A chest radiograph is clear. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin4.6 g/dL (baseline 8.2 g/dL)
Mean corpuscular volume91 fL
Leukocyte count9,800/µL
Platelet count285,000/µL
Reticulocyte count0.4% (baseline 11%)
Aminotransferases (AST, ALT)Normal
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his worsening anemia?
questions.explanation: People with sickle cell disease normally have a high reticulocyte count, and when hemolysis worsens, a working marrow drives the count even higher as it tries to replace the destroyed cells. A sharp fall in hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count should make you think of an aplastic crisis, classically from parvovirus B19, which halts red-cell production. That is why the CBC and reticulocyte count are central in any acute anemia; the CBC also screens for thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration, absent here.

why_not.A: Splenic sequestration lowers the platelet count and enlarges the spleen; his platelets are normal and the spleen is not palpable.
why_not.B: Hepatic sequestration presents with an enlarging liver and abnormal liver tests, which are absent.
why_not.D: Increased hemolysis would be met by a rising reticulocyte count from a working marrow, not 0.4%.
why_not.E: Acute chest syndrome requires a new pulmonary infiltrate with chest or respiratory symptoms; his chest radiograph is clear and his oxygenation is normal.

questions.pearl: Sickle cell patients should have high reticulocytes—acute anemia with a low reticulocyte count suggests aplastic crisis; think parvovirus B19.

questions.topic: Progressive acute chest syndrome
questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) was admitted 3 days ago with a vaso-occlusive crisis involving his back, chest wall, and legs; the admission chest radiograph was clear. On hospital day 2 his hemoglobin fell from 8.1 to 6.4 g/dL, and he received 2 units of red cells (post-transfusion hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL). Today he has a temperature of 38.9 °C, worsening pleuritic chest pain, and increasing dyspnea. Respiratory rate is 32/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on ambient air and 88% on 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Crackles are heard at both lung bases, and a chest radiograph shows new bilateral lower-lobe opacities. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin have been started, he is using incentive spirometry, and his pain is managed with a morphine PCA. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin7.0 g/dL
Hemoglobin S70%
Leukocyte count19,800/µL
Platelet count172,000/µL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Simple transfusion of 2 more units of red cells
options.B: Exchange transfusion to hemoglobin S below 30%
options.D: Intravenous normal saline increased to 200 mL/h

questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is a clinical diagnosis—typically hypoxemia, dyspnea, and chest pain with a new pulmonary infiltrate—and often appears after a normal initial chest radiograph. It is the leading cause of death in adults with SCD and typically develops in the midst of a painful episode. His syndrome is progressing: fever, rising oxygen requirements with hypoxemia despite 6 L of oxygen, new bilateral infiltrates, and a hemoglobin falling despite a recent simple transfusion. The indicated step is exchange transfusion to lower hemoglobin S below 30%, while antibiotics, oxygen, and incentive spirometry continue.

why_not.A: He has progressed despite a simple transfusion; exchange transfusion is needed to bring hemoglobin S below 30%.
why_not.C: Fever, pleuritic pain, and new infiltrates indicate acute chest syndrome rather than volume overload, and diuresis does not lower hemoglobin S.
why_not.D: Aggressive IV saline risks fluid overload with pulmonary edema in SCD and does not treat acute chest syndrome.
why_not.E: Glucocorticoids are not part of recommended treatment for acute chest syndrome and do not lower the hemoglobin S fraction.

questions.pearl: Progressing acute chest syndrome—worsening hypoxemia, new infiltrates, falling hemoglobin despite simple transfusion—calls for exchange transfusion to hemoglobin S <30%.

questions.topic: Preventing acute chest syndrome during a pain crisis
questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) is admitted with a vaso-occlusive crisis causing pain in her lower ribs, upper back, and thighs. With a hydromorphone PCA her pain has improved to 5/10. She is alert, eating and drinking well, and has normal urine output. Temperature is 37.1 °C, blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, respiratory rate is 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on ambient air. The lungs are clear, and the admission chest radiograph showed no infiltrates.
questions.question: Which of the following interventions is most likely to reduce her risk of developing acute chest syndrome during this admission?

options.D: Reduced PCA dosing to avoid hypoventilation

questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in adults with SCD and usually arises in the midst of a painful episode, so prevention belongs in every VOC admission. Incentive spirometry can prevent the atelectasis and infiltrates of acute chest syndrome in patients hospitalized with chest or back pain above the diaphragm—her exact pain pattern. Because she is drinking well, fluids should be oral; patients kept on high-rate IV saline develop fluid overload with edema around the lungs.

why_not.A: She is drinking well; high-rate IV saline is unnecessary and risks fluid overload with pulmonary edema.
why_not.B: Supplemental oxygen is for hypoxemia, and her oxygen saturation is 97% on ambient air.
why_not.C: Antibiotics treat established acute chest syndrome and are not given prophylactically to an afebrile patient with a clear chest radiograph.
why_not.D: She is alert with a normal respiratory rate, and adequate analgesia rather than reduced dosing is the goal in a pain crisis.

questions.pearl: Chest or back pain during a VOC admission: incentive spirometry while awake to prevent acute chest syndrome—and oral, not excessive IV, fluids.

questions.topic: Immediate action after defibrillation
questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease was admitted with hyperkalemia after missing hemodialysis; he was dialyzed 8 hours ago, and potassium has not been rechecked since. A rapid response is called because he is unresponsive. You find him not breathing and without a palpable pulse. A code blue is called, CPR is started, and defibrillator pads are applied. At the first rhythm check, the monitor shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 180/min, and there is still no pulse. A 200-J biphasic shock is delivered.
questions.question: Which of the following should be done immediately after the shock?

options.C: Push calcium chloride and await its effect

questions.explanation: After a shock, resume CPR immediately: compressions restart without a pulse or rhythm check, and the next rhythm check comes after 2 minutes. Interruptions should be minimized, no more than 10 seconds per rhythm and pulse check; simply continuing compressions is one of the most modifiable parts of a good resuscitation. Suspected reversible causes, such as hyperkalemia in a patient who missed dialysis, are treated concurrently with CPR rather than during a pause.

why_not.A: A pulse check right after the shock interrupts compressions; pulse and rhythm are checked at the 2-minute interval.
why_not.B: The rhythm is reassessed after 2 minutes of CPR, not immediately after the shock.
why_not.C: Reversible causes are treated during CPR; compressions should not stop to wait for a drug's effect.
why_not.D: Airway placement should not interrupt compressions; bag-mask ventilation continues in the meantime.

questions.pearl: Shock, then straight back on the chest: 2 minutes of CPR before the next rhythm check, and treat reversible causes without pausing compressions.

questions.topic: Hypertensive flash pulmonary edema before IV access
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%), COPD, and chronic kidney disease was admitted 10 days ago for a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with PCI; he developed acute kidney injury and started hemodialysis 3 days ago but still makes urine. At 8 PM he develops acute dyspnea. Sign-out reported that today's dialysis went well, but the nurse tells you it was stopped early because of transient hypotension. He is alert and speaking in short phrases. Blood pressure is 212/124 mm Hg, heart rate is 112/min, respiratory rate is 32/min, and oxygen saturation is 85% on room air, improving to 90% with a nonrebreather mask. There are diffuse crackles with scattered expiratory wheezes. Fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL. His only intravenous catheter has infiltrated; a nurse is placing a new line, and respiratory therapy is bringing a noninvasive ventilator.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension, hypoxemia, and diffuse crackles after an aborted dialysis session point to flash pulmonary edema. While oxygen is given and noninvasive ventilation is set up, the fastest way to drop preload and afterload is sublingual nitroglycerin from the crash cart (for example, 2–3 tablets of 400 mcg), which does not require IV access. IV furosemide follows once access is obtained, along with aggressive blood-pressure control and likely ICU transfer.

why_not.B: The wheezes reflect pulmonary edema; a bronchodilator does not unload the ventricle.
why_not.C: An oral diuretic acts too slowly for flash pulmonary edema; give IV furosemide once access is obtained.
why_not.D: Beta-blockade does not rapidly unload the ventricle and can depress contractility in decompensated heart failure.
why_not.E: He is hypertensive and volume overloaded; the earlier transient hypotension does not mean he needs fluid now.

questions.pearl: Flash pulmonary edema with severe hypertension: sublingual nitroglycerin from the crash cart works before IV access — then IV loop diuretic.

questions.topic: Hierarchy of evidence
questions.stem: A hospitalist preparing for journal club wants the strongest available evidence on whether a new medication reduces 30-day readmissions after hospitalization for heart failure. Her literature search identifies several sources that address the question.
questions.question: Which of the following sources provides the strongest evidence?

options.A: A guideline based on a survey of experts chosen by its authors
options.B: A prospective cohort study of 4,000 patients
options.C: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials
options.D: A case-control study using medical records
options.E: A case series of three patients

questions.explanation: On the evidence pyramid, the top is the strongest form of evidence, and systematic reviews are considered one of the strongest forms. Below the filtered information is unfiltered information, led by randomized controlled trials. Cohort studies are observational and not as reliable as trials because the groups may differ; case-control studies and background evidence or expert opinion sit lower. A guideline is only as strong as its foundation: one built on systematic reviews is much stronger than one formulated from expert opinion.

why_not.A: A guideline formulated from hand-picked experts' opinions rests on the base of the pyramid and is weaker than one built on systematic reviews.
why_not.B: Cohort studies are observational and less reliable than randomized trials because the groups may differ.
why_not.D: Case-control studies rely on medical records and recall and cannot show causation.
why_not.E: Case series are useful for rare conditions but lack statistical validity.

questions.pearl: Climb the pyramid: systematic reviews > randomized trials > cohort > case-control > case reports > expert opinion.

questions.topic: Formulating an answerable PICO question
questions.stem: A resident caring for adults hospitalized with alcohol withdrawal wonders whether phenobarbital works better than lorazepam. Before she searches PubMed, her attending asks her to rewrite the idea as an answerable clinical question.
questions.question: Which of the following is the best-formulated clinical question?

options.A: In hospitalized adults with alcohol withdrawal, does phenobarbital versus lorazepam reduce ICU transfers?
options.B: What is the best way to treat alcohol withdrawal in adults who are admitted to the hospital?
options.C: In hospitalized adults with alcohol withdrawal, how do patients and nurses feel about receiving phenobarbital?
options.D: Is phenobarbital or lorazepam the better drug for treating alcohol withdrawal in hospitalized adults?
options.E: Among adults hospitalized with alcohol withdrawal who receive phenobarbital, what proportion need ICU transfer?

questions.explanation: An answerable question lets you know when you have the answer. The PICO format names the Population (patient or problem), the Intervention, the Comparison, and the Outcome—all four in one sentence—and the outcome should be measurable wherever possible. The keyed question specifies hospitalized adults with alcohol withdrawal (P), phenobarbital (I), lorazepam (C), and ICU transfer (O), so it can be searched and answered.

why_not.B: "The best way to treat" names no intervention, comparison, or measurable outcome, so you would not know when you had the answer.
why_not.C: It names no comparison and asks open-endedly how people feel rather than specifying a defined, measurable outcome.
why_not.D: It names a population, intervention, and comparison, but "better" is not a measurable outcome.
why_not.E: Without a comparison group, it can describe outcomes on phenobarbital but cannot show whether phenobarbital beats lorazepam.

questions.pearl: Write PICO in one sentence with a measurable outcome—if you can't measure it, you won't know when you've found the answer.

questions.topic: Distressing low sexual desire after menopause
questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman is evaluated for 18 months of low sexual desire that she finds distressing. Her final menstrual period was 5 years ago, and her hot flashes have resolved. She has no vaginal dryness or pain with intercourse and describes a supportive relationship. PHQ-9 score is 2, and she takes no medications. She and her partner completed several sessions of sex therapy without improvement. Pelvic examination is normal, without signs of vaginal atrophy. She asks about medication.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Reassurance that low desire is expected after menopause

questions.explanation: Her distressing low desire persists despite sex therapy, and depression, genitourinary symptoms, medications, and relationship problems have been excluded. In postmenopausal women, testosterone has positive effects on sexual desire. It is given transdermally—off-label in the United States—typically as about one-tenth of a male transdermal gel dose, with a serum testosterone level checked to avoid excessive levels; counsel about acne and hirsutism. Avoid pellets: their testosterone delivery is very variable and they are not proven to work.

why_not.A: Her low desire is distressing, and testosterone has evidence of benefit for low libido after menopause.
why_not.C: Pellets deliver testosterone very variably and are not proven to work.
why_not.D: Systemic estrogen plus progestogen has no robust evidence of benefit for libido, and she has no vasomotor symptoms to treat.
why_not.E: Vaginal estradiol targets genitourinary symptoms of menopause, which she does not have.

questions.pearl: For distressing low libido after menopause, consider low-dose transdermal testosterone with serum level monitoring—not pellets.

questions.topic: Midlife insomnia without vasomotor symptoms
questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 months of difficulty staying asleep. She falls asleep easily but wakes around 3 AM at least 4 nights per week, cannot get back to sleep, and feels unrefreshed and fatigued during the day. Her final menstrual period was 2 years ago. She has no hot flashes or night sweats. She does not snore, her partner has not observed pauses in breathing, and she has no urge to move her legs at night. She drinks one cup of coffee each morning and no alcohol. PHQ-9 score is 3, and BMI is 23. A friend told her that hormone therapy fixed her own sleep, and she asks about starting it.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Sleep disturbance in the menopause transition typically looks like this: falling asleep is fine, but there are nighttime awakenings with trouble getting back to sleep and unrefreshing sleep. Without vasomotor symptoms, hormone therapy is not an evidence-based primary treatment for sleep disturbance. Assess for primary sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea and restless legs syndrome (neither is suggested here), then treat the insomnia itself: CBT for insomnia is the gold-standard management.

why_not.B: Polysomnography is for suspected primary sleep disorders such as sleep apnea, which her history does not suggest.
why_not.C: Gabapentin is an option for restless legs syndrome or hot flashes, neither of which she has.
why_not.D: Without vasomotor symptoms, hormone therapy is not an evidence-based primary treatment for sleep disturbance.
why_not.E: A hypnotic is not first-line; CBT for insomnia is the gold-standard initial treatment.

questions.pearl: Midlife insomnia without hot flashes: screen for sleep apnea and restless legs, then refer for CBT-I rather than prescribing hormones.

questions.topic: Hair thinning after menopause
questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 years of gradually thinning hair over the crown with a widening central part; her frontal hairline is preserved. Her final menstrual period was 6 years ago, and she has no hot flashes. She has no acne or hirsutism. For 6 months she has taken a high-dose biotin "hair, skin, and nails" supplement without benefit. Scalp examination shows diffuse thinning over the crown without scarring, scale, or erythema. Ferritin level and thyroid function tests obtained before she started the supplement were normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.C: Topical estradiol applied to the scalp
options.E: Topical tretinoin applied to the scalp

questions.explanation: Menopause-associated hair thinning is treated the same way as at any other time of life: topical minoxidil, the only FDA-approved medication. Hormone therapy may offer some benefit for hair, but hair loss is not a primary indication to start systemic hormone therapy. Estrogen applied to the scalp does not help; local estrogen is reserved for genitourinary syndrome of menopause. There is insufficient evidence to recommend biotin for hair, and it can affect laboratory test results.

why_not.A: There is insufficient evidence for biotin for hair, and it can interfere with laboratory tests.
why_not.B: Hair loss alone is not an indication to start systemic hormone therapy.
why_not.C: Estrogen applied to the scalp does not help; local estrogen is reserved for genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
why_not.E: Topical tretinoin is a photoaging treatment and is not an established therapy for hair thinning.

questions.pearl: Menopausal hair thinning: topical minoxidil is the only FDA-approved medication; biotin and hormones are not the answer.

questions.topic: Cognitive complaints ("brain fog") in the menopause transition
questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is evaluated for 8 months of forgetfulness. She has trouble finding words and remembering names and is more easily distracted at work, and she worries that she is developing dementia. Her menstrual periods have become irregular over the past year. She has no hot flashes or night sweats, sleeps 7 to 8 hours nightly, and screens negative for depression and anxiety. She is independent in all activities. She asks whether she should start hormone therapy or an omega-3 supplement. Neurologic examination is normal, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 29/30. TSH and vitamin B12 levels are normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Word-finding trouble, forgetfulness, and distractibility ("brain fog") during the menopause transition are real but almost always reversible and temporary. With a normal examination and cognitive screen, validation and reassurance go a long way, along with evidence-based brain-health strategies: exercise, a Mediterranean diet, managing metabolic risk factors, substance moderation, and social and cognitive engagement. Treating vasomotor symptoms, poor sleep, or mood changes can help cognition when present, but for isolated cognitive symptoms, hormone therapy has little impact.

why_not.A: Her symptoms are typical, reversible menopause-related changes with a normal cognitive screen, not dementia.
why_not.B: There is no good evidence that brain supplements such as omega-3 improve cognition, and supplements are not FDA-reviewed for safety or effectiveness before sale.
why_not.D: For isolated cognitive symptoms without vasomotor symptoms, hormone therapy has little impact.
why_not.E: Isoflavones have only small, poor-quality studies that cannot reliably guide treatment.

questions.pearl: Menopausal brain fog is real and temporary: validate, address hot flashes, sleep, and mood, and promote brain-healthy habits—not supplements.

questions.topic: 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with acute onset of left facial droop and slurred speech. She reports 3 weeks of generalized weakness and night sweats. She has a fractured molar that she has not been able to have repaired. The day before presentation, she noticed a painful red nodule on the pad of a finger. She has no known heart disease, prosthetic material, or history of injection drug use. Temperature is 38.3 °C and heart rate 104/min. No cardiac murmur is heard. Head CT shows an acute right middle cerebral artery territory infarct. Three of 3 blood culture sets grow Streptococcus mitis. Echocardiography has not yet been performed.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes her status under the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria?
questions.explanation: Major: in the 2023 update, any streptococcus except S. pneumoniae or group A strep is a typical endocarditis pathogen, so S. mitis in multiple blood cultures is a major criterion; there is no imaging major criterion yet because echocardiography is pending. Minor: fever, an embolic (vascular) phenomenon—her stroke—and an immunologic phenomenon, the Osler node. The fractured molar is a risk factor but not a predisposition minor criterion. Definite endocarditis requires 2 major, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria.

why_not.A: S. mitis, like any streptococcus other than S. pneumoniae or group A strep, is a major criterion when it grows in multiple blood cultures.
why_not.B: The stroke (vascular) and the painful finger-pad nodule (immunologic) both count, along with fever, giving three minor criteria.
why_not.C: The fractured molar is a risk factor for bacteremia, not a predisposition minor criterion.
why_not.E: A cerebral infarct is a vascular minor criterion; imaging major criteria come from cardiac imaging, which has not been done.

questions.pearl: 2023 Duke-ISCVID: any strep except S. pneumoniae/group A is typical; definite IE = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.

questions.topic: Culture-negative endocarditis
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with mitral valve prolapse and moderate mitral regurgitation has had 4 weeks of fatigue, low-grade fevers, night sweats, and a 4-kg weight loss. Ten days ago, an urgent care clinic prescribed a 7-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for presumed sinusitis; his symptoms improved briefly and then recurred. He has no animal exposures, has not consumed unpasteurized dairy products, and does not inject drugs. Temperature is 38.1 °C. He has splinter hemorrhages and an apical holosystolic murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 9-mm mobile vegetation on the mitral valve. Three blood culture sets drawn from separate venipunctures on admission show no growth after 5 days.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely reason the blood cultures are negative?

options.C: Blood cultures not drawn during fever
options.D: Too few blood culture sets obtained

questions.explanation: The most common reason for culture-negative endocarditis today is that blood cultures were obtained after antibiotics were started, sterilizing them—particularly with streptococci and other fastidious organisms. HACEK organisms were historically considered the leading cause, but modern blood culture systems now detect them. Because endocarditis causes continuous bacteremia, cultures need not be timed to fever; at least three separate sets from different peripheral sites are recommended, as he had. To prevent culture-negative endocarditis, draw cultures before antibiotics: when endocarditis is suspected in a stable patient, it is reasonable to hold antibiotics until more information is available.

why_not.A: Modern blood culture systems detect HACEK organisms, which are no longer the leading cause of culture-negative endocarditis.
why_not.B: Coxiella can cause culture-negative endocarditis, but he lacks exposures, and recent antibiotics are a far more common explanation.
why_not.C: Endocarditis causes continuous bacteremia, so cultures do not need to be timed to fever.
why_not.D: He had three separate sets from different peripheral sites, which meets the recommendation.

questions.pearl: Culture-negative endocarditis today usually means antibiotics before cultures—draw at least three sets before treating a stable patient.

questions.topic: Endocarditis prophylaxis for dental procedures
questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is scheduled for extraction of a nonrestorable molar. Two years ago he completed treatment for Streptococcus mitis tricuspid valve endocarditis related to injection drug use; his opioid use disorder has since been in sustained remission on buprenorphine. Eight months ago a dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted for sick sinus syndrome. Echocardiography shows mild tricuspid regurgitation; he has no prosthetic valve. He has no drug allergies.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis for the extraction?

options.B: Amoxicillin 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure
options.C: Azithromycin 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure
options.D: Clindamycin 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure
options.E: Amoxicillin for 5 days after the procedure

questions.explanation: Dental prophylaxis is given to high-risk patients, and prior infective endocarditis qualifies because the damaged valve can be reinfected. A pacemaker alone is not an indication, but it does not cancel his prior-endocarditis indication. The regimen is amoxicillin about 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure; cephalexin, azithromycin, or doxycycline are options only when penicillin allergy precludes amoxicillin. Good dental hygiene remains the main prevention strategy.

why_not.A: Prior infective endocarditis is a high-risk condition that warrants prophylaxis, even though his pacemaker alone would not.
why_not.C: Azithromycin is an alternative only for patients who cannot take amoxicillin because of penicillin allergy.
why_not.D: Clindamycin is no longer recommended for dental prophylaxis, and he has no penicillin allergy.
why_not.E: Prophylaxis is a single preprocedure dose, not a postprocedure course.

questions.pearl: Prior IE—not a pacemaker alone—warrants dental prophylaxis: amoxicillin 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure.

questions.topic: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis
questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman underwent surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement for a stenotic bicuspid valve 2 months ago. She now has 2 weeks of low-grade fevers, malaise, and night sweats. Temperature is 38.2 °C, blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg, and heart rate 94/min. The sternotomy incision is healed, and she has no intravenous catheter. A soft systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border is unchanged from her postoperative examination. Two of 2 blood culture sets drawn from separate venipunctures grow Staphylococcus epidermidis. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a well-seated bioprosthesis with expected gradients and no vegetation; image quality is limited by prosthetic shadowing.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.E: No further testing; treat as contamination

questions.explanation: In early prosthetic valve endocarditis, coagulase-negative staphylococci are a more common cause, so a positive culture for coagulase-negative staph in a patient with prosthetic material should be investigated rather than treated as a contaminant. TTE is much less sensitive for prosthetic valve and paravalvular infection, so a negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis—TEE is the next step. Cardiac CT and PET/CT are helpful adjuncts when concern persists, but echocardiography remains the mainstay, and they are not the first test.

why_not.B: TTE is insensitive with a prosthetic valve; waiting to repeat it delays the more sensitive TEE.
why_not.C: Cardiac CT is an adjunct—good for paravalvular complications but insensitive for vegetations—not the first test.
why_not.D: PET/CT can improve sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis but is an adjunct, not the first test.
why_not.E: With a prosthetic valve, coagulase-negative staphylococci in blood cultures warrant investigation rather than dismissal as contamination.

questions.pearl: CoNS bacteremia after recent valve replacement needs investigation, not dismissal as contamination; TTE misses prosthetic valve infection—get a TEE.

questions.topic: Hospice levels of care
questions.stem: An 87-year-old man with metastatic bladder cancer has been hospitalized for 2 weeks with recurrent hematuria requiring transfusion of 2 units of red cells. His oncologist estimates a prognosis of weeks to a month. He declines further transfusions and hospitalizations, wants to focus on comfort, and has elected hospice. The hematuria is now minimal. He has no pain, dyspnea, nausea, or agitation and has needed no as-needed medications, but he is too fatigued to walk and needs help with bathing, toileting, and transfers. Blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation on ambient air are normal. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL. He is widowed and lives alone; his only sibling lives in another state and is too ill to travel.
questions.question: Which of the following hospice arrangements is most appropriate?

options.A: General inpatient hospice care in the hospital
options.B: General inpatient care at an inpatient hospice unit
options.C: Routine hospice care in a skilled nursing facility
options.E: Routine home hospice with nurses present around the clock

questions.explanation: Hospice level of care is driven by symptoms. General inpatient (GIP) care requires a symptom burden that needs inpatient management; a patient dying comfortably—even within days—does not qualify. He therefore needs the routine level of care, which can be provided at home or in a skilled nursing facility (SNF). With no caregiver support and inability to walk, he cannot safely go home, so routine hospice in a SNF is appropriate. Counsel him that SNF room and board is not covered by hospice.

why_not.A: GIP requires symptoms that need an inpatient setting to manage; comfortable dying alone does not qualify.
why_not.B: An inpatient hospice unit provides GIP-level care, which likewise requires a symptom burden needing inpatient management.
why_not.D: Routine home hospice relies on family for most hands-on care, and he lives alone and cannot walk.
why_not.E: Routine home hospice provides intermittent nurse and aide visits with 24/7 phone support, not round-the-clock nursing.

questions.pearl: Symptoms, not prognosis, set the hospice level: GIP needs a symptom burden; comfortable patients without home caregiver support usually need routine hospice in a SNF.

questions.topic: Hospice medication coverage
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction 10% to 15%) has had four hospitalizations for volume overload in the past 6 months despite maximally tolerated guideline-directed therapy and is not a candidate for advanced therapies. He has Medicare, including a Part D drug plan, on the basis of disability. He wants to avoid further hospitalizations and is enrolling in home hospice with heart failure as his terminal diagnosis. Oral furosemide relieves his dyspnea when he becomes volume overloaded, and he asks whether he can keep taking it.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate response?

options.B: Continue furosemide, billed to his Part D drug plan
options.C: Continue furosemide at his own expense
options.E: Revoke hospice to continue diuretic therapy

questions.explanation: Hospice covers all care related to the terminal prognosis, including team visits, durable medical equipment, and medications related to the terminal prognosis. Patients should stay on medications that make them feel better; for heart failure, that often means continuing their current medications, including a diuretic that relieves dyspnea, and hospice covers it. What hospice does not cover is care unrelated to the terminal prognosis, facility room and board, and curative care.

why_not.A: Hospice does not require stopping symptom-relieving medications; diuretics that ease dyspnea in heart failure often continue.
why_not.B: Medications related to the terminal diagnosis are covered by the hospice benefit, not billed separately.
why_not.C: Furosemide is related to his terminal diagnosis, so the hospice benefit covers it.
why_not.E: Symptom-relieving treatment of the terminal illness is part of hospice care, so revocation is unnecessary.

questions.pearl: Hospice covers medications related to the terminal diagnosis—heart failure patients can keep diuretics and other drugs that make them feel better.

questions.topic: Routine home hospice services
questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with end-stage COPD who uses home oxygen has had three hospitalizations for exacerbations in the past 4 months. She is being discharged home with routine-level hospice care; her dyspnea is controlled with low-dose oral morphine and oxygen. Her daughter, who lives with her and works full time, will be her primary caregiver and asks what help hospice will provide at home.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the support routine home hospice provides?

options.A: A hospice nurse at the bedside 8 to 12 hours every day
options.B: A hospice aide who stays overnight every night
options.C: Daily home visits by a hospice physician
options.D: Ambulance transport to the emergency department when symptoms worsen
options.E: Intermittent nurse and aide visits plus 24/7 on-call support

questions.explanation: With routine home hospice, the nurse typically visits a few times a week for about an hour based on symptom severity, the aide typically visits a few times a week for about an hour for personal care, other team members visit as needed, and there is 24/7 on-call support. The other ~160 hours a week of care falls on the family. Hospice is the family’s new 911: when symptoms develop, they call hospice, which advises by phone and sends a nurse or physician if needed—the goal is to avoid returning to the hospital.

why_not.A: Routine home hospice provides intermittent nursing visits, not daily shifts of bedside nursing.
why_not.B: Under routine home care, aides make brief personal-care visits, typically a few times a week; they do not stay overnight.
why_not.C: Hospice physicians can visit when needed, but daily physician visits are not part of routine home hospice.
why_not.D: The family should call hospice first; the goal is to manage symptoms at home rather than return to the hospital.

questions.pearl: Routine home hospice: brief, intermittent nurse and aide visits plus 24/7 phone support—the family provides most care; hospice is the new 911.

questions.topic: Monoarthritis in a neutropenic patient
questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma has had 7 days of increasing pain and swelling of the right knee. Five days ago an orthopedic surgeon aspirated the knee; the synovial fluid leukocyte count was 4,600/µL (55% neutrophils) with calcium pyrophosphate crystals, and Gram stain and culture were not sent. He was treated with colchicine for pseudogout without improvement. Temperature is 37.6 °C, blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 98/min. The right knee is warm with a moderate effusion and painful range of motion; his other joints are normal. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Leukocyte count1,100/µL
Absolute neutrophil count250/µL
Hemoglobin9.6 g/dL
Platelet count96,000/µL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Increase colchicine dosing to three times daily
options.B: Intra-articular triamcinolone injection of the knee
options.C: Antinuclear antibody and anti-CCP antibody testing
options.D: Repeat arthrocentesis with Gram stain and culture

questions.explanation: In immunosuppressed patients, fever and white counts are unreliable, so septic arthritis can look bland. A synovial count of about 4,600/µL means little when he has almost no circulating neutrophils—he cannot put 50,000 cells into the joint. Crystals do not rule out septic arthritis, because many people carry CPPD crystals in their joint fluid. This nonresponding joint therefore needs Gram stain and culture, with broad antibiotic coverage while cultures are pending, tailored to the results.

why_not.A: Failure to improve on colchicine should prompt a search for infection, not escalation of crystal therapy.
why_not.B: Injecting a glucocorticoid into a joint that may be infected, before infection is excluded, risks worsening septic arthritis.
why_not.C: A new autoimmune arthritis is far less likely than infection in a neutropenic patient with a single worsening joint.
why_not.E: Systemic glucocorticoids would further mask infection and do nothing to diagnose or treat a septic joint.

questions.pearl: Crystals don't exclude a septic joint, and neutropenic patients can't mount a high synovial count—culture the nonresponding joint.

questions.topic: Scleroderma renal crisis with an apparently normal blood pressure
questions.stem:
A 46-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 14 months ago is seen in clinic. Six weeks ago she began prednisone 50 mg daily for an inflammatory myopathy. For the past 4 days she has had headache and fatigue. Her home log shows usual systolic blood pressures of 85–95 mm Hg. Today blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse is 96/min. She has diffuse skin thickening of the face, arms, and trunk, and tendon friction rubs are palpable at both ankles. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin10.0 g/dL (2 weeks ago: 11.9 g/dL)
Platelet count171,000/µL (2 weeks ago: 348,000/µL)
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL (2 weeks ago: 0.6 mg/dL)
UrinalysisTrace protein; no cells or casts
Peripheral blood smearSchistocytes, 3–4 per high-power field
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Begin captopril and titrate the dose rapidly
options.B: Begin labetalol to lower blood pressure
options.C: Recheck blood pressure and labs in 1 week
options.D: Begin plasma exchange for presumed TTP
options.E: Obtain a kidney biopsy before treatment

questions.explanation: This is scleroderma renal crisis. Risk is highest with early diffuse disease and tendon friction rubs, and prednisone is a clear trigger. Her blood pressure looks normal but is about 30 mm Hg above her baseline, and she has new microangiopathic hemolysis (falling hemoglobin and platelets, schistocytes) with a rising creatinine. Treatment is an ACE inhibitor, started now and titrated up until the microangiopathic hemolytic anemia resolves; calcium channel blockers can be added if needed, but beta-blockers should be avoided.

why_not.B: Beta-blockers should be avoided in scleroderma renal crisis; ACE inhibition is the specific, life-saving treatment.
why_not.C: Waiting is dangerous because her blood pressure is well above her own baseline with active microangiopathic hemolysis, so treatment should start now.
why_not.D: Renal crisis can mimic TTP, but early diffuse scleroderma on high-dose prednisone points to renal crisis, which is treated with an ACE inhibitor.
why_not.E: Kidney biopsy is seldom needed and can look nearly identical to TTP; the diagnosis is clinical and treatment should not wait.

questions.pearl: Early diffuse scleroderma on prednisone: a 'normal' BP above baseline plus MAHA is renal crisis—start and up-titrate an ACE inhibitor; avoid beta-blockers.

questions.topic: Critical digital ischemia in systemic sclerosis
questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (anticentromere antibody positive), Raynaud phenomenon, and previous small digital ulcers ran out of tadalafil 1 week ago but has continued amlodipine. Yesterday, after shoveling snow for an hour, her left index finger became throbbing and dark. She presents 24 hours later with severe, constant pain. The fingertip is dusky purple and cool and remains discolored after 30 minutes of rewarming; there is no ulceration or gangrene. Radial and ulnar pulses are normal, and her other fingers show her usual color changes that resolve with warming. Vital signs are normal, and an electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Restart tadalafil and reassess in 1 week
options.B: Admit for an intravenous prostacyclin infusion
options.D: Apply topical nitroglycerin and discharge home

questions.explanation: Critical digital ischemia is a blue or purple digit that does not reverse with rewarming; unlike Raynaud phenomenon, it can be irreversible and may rapidly progress to gangrene, so it is a medical emergency. The patient should be admitted for an IV prostanoid, which promotes vasodilation and also decreases platelet aggregation, together with adequate analgesia. If prostacyclin and analgesia do not work, options include escalating vasodilators and injecting botulinum toxin into the finger.

why_not.A: Restarting an oral vasodilator and waiting a week is outpatient Raynaud care, whereas a digit that stays ischemic after rewarming is an emergency.
why_not.C: High-dose glucocorticoids do not treat scleroderma digital vasculopathy and can trigger scleroderma renal crisis.
why_not.D: Topical nitrates at home are inadequate for a digit that remains ischemic after rewarming; she needs admission and IV prostanoid therapy.
why_not.E: Amputation is reserved for nonviable tissue, and this digit is still potentially salvageable with prostanoid therapy and analgesia.

questions.pearl: A digit that stays blue or purple after rewarming is critical ischemia—an emergency: admit for an IV prostanoid plus adequate analgesia.
