questions.topic: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome
questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man with primary antiphospholipid syndrome (positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies) and a prior deep venous thrombosis stopped taking warfarin 2 weeks ago when he ran out of tablets. Over the past 3 days he has developed confusion, right-hand weakness, a lacy violaceous rash on his legs, painful dusky toes, and decreased urine output. Blood pressure is 172/98 mm Hg and pulse is 104/min. MRI of the brain shows multiple small acute infarcts. Troponin is elevated, and echocardiography shows new regional wall-motion abnormalities without valvular vegetations. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin10.6 g/dL
Platelet count62,000/µL
Creatinine2.7 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
INR1.1
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
questions.explanation: Catastrophic APS is multiorgan small-vessel thrombosis occurring over a very short period, with onset usually less than 1 week—here involving brain, heart, kidneys, and skin. Triggers include infection, surgery, malignancy, and stopped or interrupted anticoagulation, as in this patient. First-line treatment is triple therapy: anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange or IVIG, while resolving any trigger. Rituximab or eculizumab is used when patients do not respond.

why_not.A: Anticoagulation alone is inadequate first-line therapy for catastrophic APS; combination triple therapy is needed.
why_not.B: Anticoagulation is a core component of first-line triple therapy, and thrombocytopenia from consumptive thrombosis is not a reason to withhold it.
why_not.D: Rituximab is reserved for patients who do not respond to triple therapy; first-line therapy pairs anticoagulation and high-dose steroids with plasma exchange or IVIG.
why_not.E: Eculizumab is reserved for patients who do not respond to triple therapy and does not replace glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange or IVIG.

questions.pearl: Catastrophic APS: anticoagulation + high-dose steroids + plasma exchange or IVIG; rituximab or eculizumab only if refractory.

questions.topic: Microangiopathic hemolysis with thrombocytopenia
questions.stem:
A 64-year-old woman is admitted with 3 weeks of left upper quadrant pain, fatigue, and weight loss. CT shows a splenic infarct and multiple liver masses; a liver biopsy is pending, and metastatic adenocarcinoma is suspected. Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin prophylaxis was started on admission; she had no prior heparin exposure. On hospital day 3 she has oozing from venipuncture sites and new ecchymoses. She is alert and oriented; temperature is 37.3 °C, blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 98/min. Laboratory results (day 1 → day 3) are shown.
TestResult
Hemoglobin10.9 → 8.6 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume88 fL
Platelet count142,000 → 38,000/µL
INR1.1 → 1.3
Fibrinogen290 → 96 mg/dL
D-dimer (day 3)>20 µg/mL FEU (reference <0.5)
Lactate dehydrogenase (day 3)1,320 U/L (reference 140–280)
Haptoglobin (day 3)<10 mg/dL (reference 30–200)
Direct antiglobulin testNegative
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Peripheral blood smear (day 3)Schistocytes, 3–4 per high-power field
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes, high LDH, and absent haptoglobin with thrombocytopenia are not specific for TTP—DIC can show schistocytes, though it need not. The discriminator is the coagulopathy: TTP does not have a coagulopathy, whereas here the fibrinogen is falling (an acute-phase reactant, so track the trend) with a very high D-dimer. DIC is a 'thrombin explosion': excess tissue factor from cancer, sepsis, or trauma sets off the coagulation cascade, and her suspected metastatic adenocarcinoma is the likely driver.

why_not.A: TTP does not cause a coagulopathy, and a fibrinogen falling to 96 mg/dL with a very high D-dimer points to DIC.
why_not.B: The platelet fall began within 3 days of her first-ever heparin exposure and has another clear cause, giving a low 4Ts score.
why_not.C: Evans syndrome combines autoimmune hemolytic anemia with immune thrombocytopenia, but her direct antiglobulin test is negative and schistocytes indicate mechanical hemolysis.
why_not.D: Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated thrombocytopenia without schistocytes, hemolysis, or coagulopathy.

questions.pearl: Schistocytes plus low platelets isn't automatically TTP—a falling fibrinogen (track the trend) means DIC; TTP has no coagulopathy.

questions.topic: Suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man was admitted 7 days ago with acute decompensated heart failure and has been treated with intravenous furosemide and subcutaneous unfractionated heparin 5,000 units every 8 hours for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. He had no heparin exposure in the past year, and his home medications are unchanged. He feels better and has no fever, bleeding, limb swelling, or skin lesions at injection sites. Hemoglobin and leukocyte count are unchanged. A PF4–heparin antibody immunoassay has been sent. Platelet counts are shown.
TestResult
Platelet count, admission (day 0)252,000/µL
Platelet count, day 4238,000/µL
Platelet count, day 5214,000/µL
Platelet count, day 6151,000/µL
Platelet count, day 798,000/µL
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Continue heparin until the antibody result returns
options.C: Stop heparin and withhold all anticoagulation

questions.explanation: His 4Ts score is 6 (high probability): a >50% fall to a nadir ≥20,000/µL (2), a fall beginning on day 5 (2), no thrombosis (0), and no other apparent cause (2). With a 4Ts score of 4 or greater, stop heparin—all heparin exposure, including flushes—and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, a DOAC, or fondaparinux. Stopping heparin alone is not enough, because even HIT without thrombosis should be anticoagulated.

why_not.A: With a 4Ts score of 4 or more, heparin should be stopped now rather than after the antibody result returns.
why_not.B: Enoxaparin is a heparin, and all heparin exposure must stop when HIT is suspected.
why_not.C: Stopping heparin alone is insufficient, because even HIT without thrombosis requires a non-heparin anticoagulant.
why_not.E: Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in HIT without bleeding, and heparin must be stopped.

questions.pearl: 4Ts ≥4: stop ALL heparin (even flushes) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant—argatroban, fondaparinux, or a DOAC—even without thrombosis.

questions.topic: Unexpected thrombocytopenia in an asymptomatic patient
questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man has preoperative laboratory testing before an elective inguinal hernia repair. He feels well and has never had easy bruising or prolonged bleeding, including after a dental extraction last year. He takes no medications. Examination shows no petechiae, purpura, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Leukocyte count6,800/µL
Hemoglobin14.6 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume90 fL
Platelet count31,000/µL (2 years ago: 236,000/µL)
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: An unexpectedly low platelet count in a patient with no bleeding history and no petechiae calls first for a look at the peripheral blood smear. Pseudothrombocytopenia—platelet clumping in the sample—produces a falsely low count, and the smear is how you find it. Reviewing the smear in thrombocytopenia is routine for exactly this reason, and it also screens for a microangiopathic process. More extensive outpatient tests, such as ultrasonography for splenomegaly, come at a later stage if no answer emerges.

why_not.A: Treating presumed ITP is premature before platelet clumping has been excluded on the smear.
why_not.B: Platelet transfusion is not indicated before true thrombocytopenia is confirmed in a patient who is not bleeding.
why_not.C: A bone marrow biopsy is premature when the count has not yet been confirmed by smear review.
why_not.D: Imaging for splenomegaly belongs to a later stage of the outpatient evaluation, after the smear and basic tests.

questions.pearl: Unexpected thrombocytopenia without bleeding: look at the smear first—platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia) can mimic a dangerously low count.

questions.topic: Newly diagnosed ITP with a platelet count above 30,000/µL
questions.stem:
A 36-year-old man is referred because a routine complete blood count showed a low platelet count. He feels well. He has noticed a few pinpoint red spots around his ankles but has had no gum bleeding, nosebleeds, blood in his urine or stool, or easy bruising. He takes no medications or supplements, drinks alcohol rarely, and has had no recent illness or vaccination. A platelet count 3 years ago was 231,000/µL. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows a few scattered petechiae on both ankles and no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResult
Leukocyte count6,400/µL, normal differential
Hemoglobin15.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume88 fL
Platelet count46,000/µL (repeat 1 week later: 44,000/µL)
PT, aPTT, and liver chemistriesNormal
HIV, hepatitis B and C, and Helicobacter pylori testsNegative
Peripheral blood smearNormal red and white cells; no schistocytes; platelets decreased in number and large; no clumping
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Referral to a surgeon for elective splenectomy

questions.explanation: This is a typical presentation of ITP, a diagnosis of exclusion: isolated thrombocytopenia with no other explanation and a smear showing normal red cells, no schistocytes, and large platelets. Without significant bleeding, the decision to treat rests on the platelet count: treatment is given when it is below about 20,000–30,000/µL, but above 30,000/µL ITP is not treated. With 46,000/µL and only minor skin bleeding, he should be observed rather than treated. Routine bone marrow examination is no longer done for typical ITP; it is considered when presumed ITP does not respond to treatment.

why_not.B: ITP with a platelet count above 30,000/µL and only minor skin bleeding is not treated, so glucocorticoids are not indicated.
why_not.C: A typical ITP presentation does not require bone marrow examination, which is considered when features are atypical or presumed ITP does not respond to treatment.
why_not.D: IVIG is used when a rapid platelet rise is needed, such as with very low counts or significant bleeding, neither of which is present.
why_not.E: Splenectomy is a later option for ITP that persists despite treatment, not for a patient who needs no therapy.

questions.pearl: Typical ITP with platelets above 30,000/µL and no or minor bleeding: observe—no glucocorticoids, IVIG, or bone marrow biopsy.
